#2881. Is Jacoby Brissett playing today for Ravens? QB’s status for 'Thursday Night Football'

Jacoby Brissett's debut with the Baltimore Ravens will have to wait until next week.

In the minutes after news broke that the Ravens were finalizing a trade to acquire the veteran quarterback from the Arizona Cardinals, further reporting indicated that Brissett wouldn't be around for Baltimore's Week 9 game. According to multiple reports, the Ravens and Cardinals will not officially complete their trade until the weekend.

Baltimore head coach Jesse Minter announced Tuesday, Nov. 3 that undrafted free agent rookie Joe Fagnano would make his first career start against the Jacksonville Jaguars on "Thursday Night Football." Since Brissett won't officially join the Ravens until after the game, Fagnano is poised to remain the starter despite news of the pending transaction.

JACOBY BRISSETT: Baltimore Ravens make trade for quarterback after Lamar Jackson injury

Arizona and Baltimore were perfect trade partners for Brissett on paper.

The Cardinals benched the veteran midway through his eighth start this year after he underperformed against a poor Cowboys defense. Backup Gardner Minshew led Arizona to a comeback victory in overtime after entering the Week 8 game.

Meanwhile, the Ravens' quarterback situation was in dire straits. After Lamar Jackson sustained a thumb injury in Week 8 that would land him on injured reserve, backup Tyler "Snoop" Huntley suffered a season-ending toe injury in the same game.

Now Brissett, 33, is set to join the seventh different team of his career when the trade becomes official. Before his Cardinals stint, the veteran previously spent time with the New England Patriots, Indianapolis Colts, Miami Dolphins, Cleveland Browns and Washington Commanders.

Here's what to know about Brissett's Week 9 status ahead of "Thursday Night Football":

Brissett is not yet officially on the Ravens' roster, so he is ineligible to play for the team on "Thursday Night Football."

Baltimore will not finalize its trade for the veteran quarterback until the weekend, according to multiple reports. Until the transaction becomes official, Brissett will remain on the Cardinals' roster.

As a result, the Ravens are sticking with Fagnano, their undrafted rookie quarterback, for the start against Jacksonville on Thursday, Nov. 5. In his first career game last week, Fagnano was 10-of-21 (47.6%) passing for 91 yards and an interception against the Bills. He also rushed three times for three yards.

Brissett was having a decent start to his 2026 season before struggling against the Cowboys in Week 8. Here's how his year has looked by the numbers:

Rushing: 29 attempts for 87 yards (3.0 yards per attempt)

Baltimore has two active quarterbacks on its roster ahead of Week 9. Fagnano is the only one who has been with the Ravens since the start of the season – Slovis signed with the team on Tuesday, Nov. 3, following the injuries to Jackson and Huntley.

Both Jackson and Huntley – the Ravens' top two quarterbacks just last week – are expected to land on injured reserve in the coming days. Jackson's thumb injury requires surgery and will keep him out for at least four games. Huntley is reportedly out for the season with his turf toe injury. Skylar Thompson, whom the Ravens signed earlier this year, is also on injured reserve with an undisclosed injury.

Outside of the quarterbacks listed, Baltimore also has Austin Reed on its practice squad. Reed, who played in the UFL in the spring, was on the Ravens' training camp roster before his release ahead of the regular season. He re-signed with the Ravens' practice squad on Monday, Nov. 2.

#2879. Binance breach puts custody at center of crypto infrastructure trade

The $6.3 billion Binance hack could accelerate a shift in how investors value cryptocurrency companies, putting a greater premium on custody providers and the infrastructure needed to securely hold and protect digital assets.

Much of crypto's evolution this year has involved companies moving past their reliance on trading volumes and transaction fees, to focus instead on building the infrastructure connecting digital assets with traditional finance. Last Thursday's breach adds a new dimension, bringing cybersecurity, custody, compliance and balance-sheet resilience into sharper focus.

Importantly, the Binance breach was not an indictment of crypto itself, or a case of leadership-driven fraud, as with FTX in late 2022. Instead, Binance's leadership moved quickly to contain the fallout, protect customers and commit the exchange's own resources to cover losses.

On Tuesday, Binance CEO Richard Teng told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" that the company has replenished 98% of $6.34 billion in affected assets, and that it is still in the process of purchasing outstanding, more illiquid assets.

Management's response, alongside efforts elsewhere in the industry to boost confidence, helped prevent a security breach from escalating into a broader crisis of confidence. For example, Tether, Circle, Ripple and others moved quickly to freeze or restrict access to about $3 billion in stolen assets; Coinbase blocked transfers to compromised wallets and offered Binance direct assistance.

The hack could even help shape the next phase of the crypto infrastructure trade. The new winners may not just be the businesses with the most users, volume or assets under custody, but the ones that can also demonstrate they're able to protect those assets under extreme duress.

"Which company has the resources to invest in cybersecurity and protect customer funds? For a smaller company, it could be much harder because once these crypto companies become infrastructure plays, providing the well for tokenization … they need to have the compliance and control in place so that a similar hacking will not happen or can be minimized," Owen Lau, senior analyst at ClearStreet, told CNBC. "Larger companies have more resources that could give them some advantage."

While institutional investors have increasingly embraced digital assets, broader adoption depends on confidence that those assets can be securely held, accessed and transferred. The Binance breach highlights the importance of that infrastructure, and could increase demand for specialized custodians and platforms with established asset-protection capabilities.

Coinbase has operated a dedicated institutional custody business since 2018. Circle entered the custody business this year, after the U.S. Office of the Comptroller of the Currency granted it approval to operate as a trust bank. In the past few years, Ripple and Kraken have also launched custody businesses.

Still, smaller players compete in the space as well. Small cap crypto exchange stock Gemini Space Station has offered custody services since 2019. BitGo Holdings, founded in 2013, is one of the earliest players in institutional crypto custody and infrastructure, with a reputation for security and serving major institutions.

The shift could also drive consolidation as companies look to buy capabilities, deepen their infrastructure offerings and achieve the scale needed to compete, Lau said.

The more consequential structural shift may be the separation of custody from execution, according to Morgan Stanley.

"Crypto exchanges have historically combined trading, custody, and settlement within vertically integrated platforms, concentrating operational risk. Repeated security breaches could encourage investors to move assets toward independent custody while continuing to trade on CEXs," the firm's analyst Felix Stratmann said in a note Monday," referring to centralized cryptocurrency exchanges.

"This would preserve the role of centralized exchanges as liquidity and execution venues, while potentially benefiting regulated custodians, including banks, as institutional investors place greater emphasis on asset segregation, operational resilience, and investor protection," Stratmann said.

#2876. The Jazz Peli-can’t snap out of losing streak, their 6th straight

In the darkest, inner circle of the inferno, the Jazz had fallen into, all Jazz fans wanted was a sign of life that this team was still alive and kicking.

Missing Jusuf Nurkic and Jaren Jackson Jr. with an uncertain timetable, a 1-7 start would be detrimental. They've battled against top dogs like the Spurs, Blazers and Grizzlies, meaning this was one of the few chances to bounce back as the worst team in the West. Utah had already taken down the Pelicans in their home opener, marking their first and only win on the season.

New Orleans had been on their own soul-searching journey in their 2026-27 campaign. They lost their first four games on the calendar, three of them coming up short in the clutch. But now, their record stands at 3-4; they handed Memphis their first loss of the year while taking down the Mavs and Kings on the side.

But unfortunately, that well-sought victory was not today. It was certainly the most alive the Jazz have looked all week, but ultimately they still fell into the same lapses that have plagued them all season. The Pelicans stole this one out of the Jazz's hands, 120-113.

The pace was all over the place in the first quarter. There was even a 2-minute scoring drought for both teams midway through the early going, an early indicator that Utah was going to start yet another game ice-cold from the floor. There are times when you just have to sigh at the Jazz's attempt to run an offense — using traditional big men as playmaking hubs, force-feeding players when they don't have the hot hand, and just the lack of team synergy that leads to a possession ending with a shot-chuck at the buzzer. Fortunately, at the hand of Keyonte George, the Jazz answered back to erase an 8-point deficit. They switched away from the three-point line to score 18 of their first 20 points inside the paint.

Then, it was Saddiq Bey's second quarter. He scored eight consecutive points for New Orleans to give the Pelicans a crescive 9-point lead. Utah missed seven consecutive shots to open up that quarter. It was another ugly one; the lackadaisical passes destroyed any rhythm the Jazz could build. Really, one of the bigger silver linings was holding Zion scoreless in the first half. 2-20 from three. 3-8 from the charity stripe. 13 turnovers. A big energy shift was needed.

And a shift it was. The dynamic went nearly completely in Utah's favor, turning around what was a tight deficit into a 10-point advantage. George jumpstarted the engine of the offense, pushing his game total to 29. Led by Mo Bamba's intimidating presence off the bench, the Jazz dominated he glass. Utah out-rebounded New Orleans 38 to 31 up until that point, dropping the Pelicans' second-chance points to 5 in the third quarter.

But I'd be lying if I said the Jazz could sit back and ride out a confident double-digit victory. New Orleans instantly opened on a 16-2 run to erase Utah's advantage. Hardy called a timeout about three possessions too late, fuelling the fire for the Pelicans. The two teams battled neck and neck over the next few minutes. A Keyonte floater. Zion free throws. Keyonte and-1. Derik Queen drive. Jaxson Hayes two. The Jazz held a nailbiting 102-102 lead with the final play, then:

The cruel joke played on the Jazz was that George let go of the ball 0.1 seconds too late. We're headed to OT.

That seemed to light a fire in him, as Keyonte nailed the first two buckets in the overtime period off tough three-point looks. The Pelicans responded with six unanswered points; the Jazz stood no chance against the physicality of Zion and Bey. There were some serious moments in this stretch that questioned whether Will Hardy's job was on the line (which seems to be the consensus).

The Jazz are firmly positioned in their last spot in the Western Conference, falling well into the lottery delegation zone; their pick was traded to the Grizzlies in the Jackson Jr. trade. While the losses are looming, the competetive nature of the fourth quarter is a fight we needed. Whether the rest will come is still under debate.

It was a rough two-game stretch for Keyonte, resulting in consecutive blowouts, but he had success tonight by dealing most of his damage inside, using his speed to attack the paint and finish with contact at the rim. He was highly disruptive on the defensive end too, chipping in four steals and an unexpected block.

It's nearly an undeniable fact that Keyonte has had to be 'the man' nearly every single night among his peers' shooting droughts. He's taken a noticable leap forward as a lead scorer and a focal point of the offense when others have missed time with injury. He looks much more confident creating his own shot and initiating the offense compared to last year.

To float in the Western Conference, this team desperately needs a second initiator/scorer. Wins won't come off Keyonte alone.

There was no other way to describe Ace on the scoring end in this one other than an unfortunate shooting night. While he played relatively well inside the arc, he spent all game searching for his rhythm from deep, having missed all 8 of his 9 of his three-point attempts. He got the looks he wanted, but couldn't take advantage. Ace finished with 15 points, 5 boards and a block on 6-for-14 shooting.

Though it's not all doom and gloom. Beyond the box score, Ace's physical presence showed in his off-ball activity. The team used him frequently to absorb switches on the perimeter and cut off driving angles for the monster of muscle, otherwise known as Zion Williamson.

A point of growth in his game has been managing his eagerness to jump at ball fakes. Tonight, he displayed a more grounded, disciplined stance and relied on his standing reach to contest shots without overcommitting. The motor is awesome to watch, no matter how he's playing on the other end of the floor.

Utah drops to 1-7 with this loss and lines up their next matchup in Dallas on Friday night.

#2875. Dalton Knecht 'came in ready to go' in Knicks debut: 'It was great'

Wednesday's game was the perfect chance for head coach Mike Brown to have Dalton Knecht make his Knicks debut.

After being waived by the Los Angeles Lakers, New York signed Knecht to a two-way contract roughly two weeks ago -- the 25-year-old had been playing with the Westchester Knicks in the NBA G League to learn the team's systems and get consistent playing time.

With the Knicks facing the 1-6 Chicago Bulls at Madison Square Garden, the team decided to make Knecht active. So when the small forward checked in for Andre Drummond with 3:20 left in the second quarter and New York up, 70-39, he was ready.

"I wasn't surprised, I just came in ready to go," Knecht said. "The coaches said you're active so that just means be ready."

Knecht got off to a great start less than a minute into his debut by following a three-point miss by Landry Shamet, grabbing the offensive rebound, and slamming it home for a putback dunk that got the MSG crowd buzzing.

"It was great. Honestly I didn't hear much just because I'm so locked in, but it was good," Knecht said about his nifty play. "Pretty much my first play was a putback dunk so it's cool, it's great."

Including his high-flying highlight, Knecht had 10 points on 4-for-6 shooting from the field, including two threes, and grabbed seven boards in just 16 minutes. He also had an assist and a block, looking good and reminding everybody why he was the 17th overall pick in the 2024 NBA Draft.

"I think I just go out there and impact the game on all three levels," Knecht said. "And I just wanna show on the other side of the ball, getting the ball pressure and stuff like that and going in and grabbing defensive rebounds."

It's hard to glean too much from Knecht's performance with it coming in a blowout against the hapless Bulls, but it's still good to see the talent is there. After all, in his rookie season, Knecht averaged 9.1 points and 2.8 rebounds in 19.2 minutes per game before taking a step back last season.

It's unclear how Brown plans to utilize Knecht this season, but as he gets more comfortable with his new team and teammates, he could be a good option for a team always looking for bench depth.

No matter what, Knecht is staying ready to make the most out of his fresh start.

"Be ready so you don't have to get ready," he said. "Just watching on the bench and talking to my teammates is really helpful and it was easy to get in there and play confident. All the guys out there gave me a good look."

Many NFL games are broadcast on local channels, so if you're looking to catch an in-market game, it may be as simple as turning on your TV (or setting up a digital TV antenna) or finding a live TV streaming service that carries the correct RSN (Regional Sports Network). A $7 monthly subscription to NFL+ will let you watch every local and primetime game live on your phone — but only a select few regular-season games on your TV. You could also spring for the uber-expensive NFL Sunday Ticket package to get every out-of-market Sunday game of the season.

When it comes to nationally broadcast games, the NFL typically airs on ESPN, NBC, CBS, FOX, ABC, and NFL Network. Thursday Night Football games stream exclusively on Amazon Prime Video; select football games stream exclusively on Peacock; games on CBS stream live on Paramount+ Premium; and select games stream on ESPN's App this season. For those keeping count, that's six channels and four streaming platforms to keep up with this season. Plus, Netflix is once again hosting at least two Christmas Day matches, a playoff game, and the first-ever Thanksgiving Eve match, so don't forget to add that subscription into the mix.

Confused? You're not alone. Here's a breakdown of the platforms we recommend checking out ahead of the 2026 NFL season, so that come game time, tuning into your favorite team's games will be as easy as simply turning on the TV.

To recap, here are all the ways you can watch NFL games in 2026.

YouTube TV gets you nearly every channel you need to watch the NFL, including Fox, NBC, ABC, CBS, ESPN and NFL Network. Plus, YouTube TV is the home of NFL Sunday Ticket. The Sunday Ticket package, while pricey on its own, gets you ALL the Sunday out-of-market games (160+ games per season).

Current pricing for new users for the 2026 Sunday Ticket is $30/month for eight months. Factor in the cost of YouTube TV's Sports and News plan at $49.99/month for your first five months, then $71.99/month thereafter.

That's $79.99/month for five months of YouTube TV + NFL Sunday Ticket, and $101.99/month for the following three months. You can also opt, with or without a YouTube TV subscription, to pay for the rest of the season of Sunday Ticket upfront for just $240.

Fubo's Sports+ News package gives you access to ESPN, NFL Network, Fox, ABC, CBS, NBC, and 20+ more live channels. Starting at $54.99/month for your first month, the live TV streaming service is definitely pricey (though certainly not the most expensive option on this list), but it offers most channels you'll need to watch both the NFL preseason and regular season.

DirecTV's Choice tier (currently $104.98/month after fees for your first three months) gets you access to nearly every channel you need to watch NFL games throughout the year: NFL Network, ESPN, NBC, CBS, Fox, SEC Network, and an abundance of local RSNs. DirecTV Choice (and most other DirecTV plans) also come with free ESPN Unlimited, which gets you access to every ESPN channel, an amazing value and a must for watching tons of college and pro sports all year round.

Amazon Prime Video is home to the NFL's Thursday Night Football. On top of Amazon Prime Video, an Amazon Prime subscription includes free shipping, exclusive deals, access to the Prime Day 2026 sale event, Amazon Music, a year of free GrubHub+ and more.

A standard Amazon Prime subscription is $15 monthly or $139 annually, but discounts are available for students and those on qualified government assistance. You can try Amazon Prime free for 30 days.

A basic $7.99 per month (or $40 annually) NFL+ subscription will get you live local and primetime regular and preseason NFL games exclusively on your phone or tablet, plus live audio for every game of the season across supported devices and access to NFL Network.

NFL+ Premium, while a little pricier at $14.99 per month (or $80 annually), also includes access to NFL RedZone, plus full and condensed replays of every game across supported devices. NFL+ also offers a 7-day free trial.

#2868. Game Recap: Suns fall to 1-5 after 132-119 loss to Trail Blazers

The Phoenix Suns began their seven-game homestand by hosting the team that obliterated them on opening night. And while the final 132-119 score wasn't nearly as embarrassing as that initial beatdown, the result was another decisive victory for Portland, which improved to 6-1 on the season and a perfect 5-0 on the road. Meanwhile, the Suns dropped to 1-5.

Devin Booker put together a solid performance, scoring 33 points, with much of his damage coming at the free-throw line, where he went a perfect 13-of-13. However, he finished with only two assists against two turnovers and struggled from beyond the arc, shooting 2-of-8. Jalen Green added 22 points, 12 of which came in the fourth quarter, although he also shot 2-of-8 from deep. Miles Bridges contributed 18 points and seven rebounds, while Dillon Brooks finished with 15 points and six rebounds.

For Portland, Donovan Clingan dominated the interior, recording 24 points and 10 rebounds on an efficient 9-of-12 shooting. Damian Lillard added 25 points, while Deni Avdija chipped in 21.

It was one of those nights when all the little things added up, and unfortunately for Phoenix, they added up to another loss. Portland won the battle in the paint, outscoring Phoenix 56-46. The Blazers controlled the second-chance points battle 17-11, dominated fast-break scoring 19-9, and received a significant advantage from their bench, which outscored the Suns' reserves 42-25. Then there was the three-point shooting. Portland connected on 14 threes at a 35.9% clip, while Phoenix managed only 10 makes on 27.8% shooting.

Across the board, the Blazers consistently found ways to win the margins that matter. When you lose that many battles within a game, it's awfully difficult to win the war.

It was a much more stable start to the game than when these teams first met on October 21. If you recall, and I'm sure you do, the Suns trailed 21–0 in that one. This time around, it took only a minute for Devin Booker to knock down an 18-foot jumper and get the scoring started for Phoenix.

The first challenge of the evening came with 8:56 remaining in the opening quarter, when Deni Avdija appeared to charge into Dillon Brooks, but a blocking foul was called on Brooks. The Suns successfully challenged the call, negating what would have been Brooks' second foul early in the game.

Phoenix looked considerably more connected on both ends of the floor throughout the first half of the opening quarter. Outside of Khaman Maluach, every starter had scored at least four points within the first six minutes, a welcome sight for a team that has struggled to find any semblance of offensive consistency.

Defensively, there were still some issues navigating the pick-and-roll, particularly with Donovan Clingan finding opportunities to score on the interior. But outside of those breakdowns, the Suns looked much more connected, communicating and rotating with a level of cohesion that had been noticeably absent in their previous meeting with Portland.

Phoenix put together a 9–2 run after the second unit entered the game, overcoming an initially choppy stretch marked by careless turnovers. Their effort on the glass was clearly a point of emphasis, and they were executing well, outrebounding Portland 13–10 in the opening quarter.

Booker came out on a heater, shooting 4-of-6 from the field for 12 first-quarter points, which is always an encouraging sign. Dillon Brooks added eight points, two rebounds, and a steal as the Suns shot 56.5% from the field while holding the Blazers to 3-of-11 from beyond the arc. The result was a 34–29 Phoenix lead heading into the second quarter.

The Trail Blazers opened the second quarter on an 11-5 run, fueled once again by Donovan Clingan, who continued attacking the interior and creating mismatches for Phoenix. Damian Lillard did his part as well, helping Portland put together an 8-0 run that further shifted the momentum.

By the midway point of the quarter, the pressure Portland was putting on Phoenix had become increasingly difficult to overcome. The Blazers were shooting 8-of-9 from the field while simultaneously drawing multiple fouls on the Suns. The offensive avalanche Phoenix had managed to avoid in the first quarter finally arrived in the second.

Portland outscored Phoenix 43-25 in the quarter, shooting 14-of-19 from the field, a ridiculous 74%, while connecting on 6-of-11 attempts from beyond the arc.

Phoenix shot 1-of-7 from deep and had 5 turnovers to the Blazers 0. Defensively, however, they reverted to the same troubling habits we've seen throughout the early portion of the season, collapsing into the paint whenever Portland attacked and leaving shooters wide open on the perimeter. And the Blazers made them pay. Jrue Holiday went 3-of-4 from beyond the arc for nine points in the quarter, Lillard added nine of his own, and Clingan chipped in eight.

Meanwhile, Booker scored seven points in the period, bringing his total to 19 at halftime. Phoenix continued to hold the advantage on the glass, but that becomes a moot point when the opposing team seemingly can't miss a shot. After experiencing an entire game's worth of shooting variance in the season opener against Portland, the Suns were treated to a quarter's worth this time around.

The Suns opened the third quarter with an offensive push, outscoring Portland 12–6 behind eight points from Devin Booker, who went 2-of-2 from the field, including a three-pointer, and 3-of-3 from the free-throw line. Portland was considerably sloppier than it had been in the second quarter, committing three turnovers as Phoenix trimmed its deficit to seven points.

In what has become a nightly tradition, Dillon Brooks found himself in a shouting match, this time with Damian Lillard, following a turnover in which Brooks stepped out of bounds in transition while attempting a three-pointer. No technicals were assessed during the exchange, but the drama wasn't finished. On Portland's ensuing possession, Brooks attempted to box out Donovan Clingan, who grabbed him by the jersey and pulled him to the floor. Officials reviewed the play for a potential hostile act, ultimately assessing Clingan a technical foul.

Jrue Holiday continued to be a menace, as the Suns repeatedly left him wide open on the perimeter, and he continued to make them pay, knocking down another pair of threes in the third quarter.

Moments later, Deni Avdija found himself under review for a potential hostile act after appearing to deliver a flying knee to Dillon Brooks' groin area. Officials ultimately ruled the contact incidental.

All those whistles started to become an issue in the third quarter, as Devin Booker, Dillon Brooks, and Jalen Green each found themselves with four fouls and four and a half minutes still remaining in the period.

Booker eventually headed to the locker room after driving to the basket and taking a shot to the head from Robert Williams. What made the sequence particularly frustrating was the inconsistency of the officiating. After spending much of the quarter calling every ticky-tack bit of contact imaginable, the officials somehow swallowed their whistles when Booker got smacked in the head. No foul. Nothing.

The lengthy third quarter mercifully came to an end, with the Suns getting outscored 32-26. Chalk up seven more fouls against Phoenix, which struggled offensively, shooting 7-of-20 from the field and a miserable 3-of-12 from two-point range. And the rebounding? That became a problem once again, as Portland dominated the glass 13–6 while scoring 18 of its 32 points in the paint.

Booker continued to lead the charge for Phoenix, pouring in 14 points in the quarter, but he finished the period in the locker room after taking that shot to the head. The Suns trailed 104-85 entering the fourth.

Devin Booker returned with 10 minutes remaining in the fourth quarter and the Suns trailing by 18 points.

With Robert Williams on the floor, Phoenix simply didn't have anyone capable of matching his size and physicality. Duop Reath was getting absolutely destroyed on the interior, as Williams grabbed four offensive rebounds in the first two minutes of the quarter alone.

We also saw Jalen Green become considerably more aggressive in the fourth, attacking the basket with a level of purpose that had been missing earlier in the game. After scoring 12 points through the first three quarters, Green shifted into attack mode, repeatedly getting downhill and creating opportunities at the free-throw line. And this time, he actually made his free throws. Miles Bridges was more engaged in the fourth quarter as well, although much like Green's performance, it felt like too little, too late.

Phoenix kept its offense humming, and there were moments when it felt like the Suns were on the verge of making a meaningful dent in Portland's lead. One sustained run could have put them within striking distance with a couple of minutes remaining. But every time Phoenix threatened to make things interesting, Portland had an answer. There was always a response. Always a reaction to the action.

With 2:51 remaining, Devin Booker fouled out for the second consecutive game, and at that point, the Suns emptied their bench. Ball game.

We are right back here tomorrow night as the Suns host the Orlando Magic, who are currently 2-5 and last played in a loss against the Wizards. We shall see you then!

#2867. INTERVIEW: Bayern boss Rouven Kasper takes swipe at Dortmund's 'Fan Mode' app as Carsten Cramer responds

MÜNCHEN (Bulinews): After Dortmund introduced a ‘Fan Mode’ feature in their club app to reward supporters staying off their phones during games, Bayern Munich's Chief Sales and Marketing officer, Rouven Kasper, said the Bavarians don't have the same issues in the stands.

“I never heard about this [BVB app] because we don’t have this problem [at Bayern Munich]. We don’t need to tell anyone to take their phone away because our football is attractive," Kasper said at a media round in Munchen, attended by Bulinews.com.

“This [Fan Mode app] is a marketing tool I have never had to think about. Maybe when you sit at home [watching a game the phone can be a problem], but I think in the Allianz Arena in Munich its not a problem.

“For sure, mobiles are there [all the time] and for when we have influencers. But in the stadium, so far, there has never been an internal discussion that we need to think about a loyalty system [to reduce phone usage].

“However, I will discuss this [fan mode app] with a colleague later, we will see what the benefits are and then maybe we will think about it," the seemingly bewildered yet intrigued 44-year-old Bayern chief concluded.

The following day, when informed about Kasper's opinions on the app, Borussia Dortmund CEO Carsten Cramer took time to defend the club's decision to put the loyalty scheme into operation.

“I know this is a kind of marketing activity [the Fan Zone app], but the marketing campaigns we develop should refer to the authenticity of the club," Cramer told Bulinews and other media present, referencing BVB's famous atmosphere.

“The emotion of is our unique selling proposition. That is our most important currency. Of course, we want to make more money to invest in sport and infrastructure, but our most important currency is the love people give us.

“The atmosphere at Signal Iduna Park is what makes Dortmund special. If you talk to the young players we signed in summer, one of their reasons for commitment was to play in front of this crowd.

“They wanted to see these fans give their emotions to them. Sometimes it’s necessary to say we have some disadvantages [compared to Bayern], and others but we really have to fight for our place [in the market].

“We are still in the top 10 [of sales] in Europe. The competitors are the big sides in England, plus the two or three [clubs] in Spain, Italy and PSG. It makes us kind of proud what we have reached in the last decade," he summarized.

#2866. Adley Rutschman’s O’s career came to an anticlimactic end

May 21, 2022. That's the day that was supposed to forever change the course of the Orioles' franchise.

It was the day that Adley Rutschman, the Orioles' wunderkind catcher, made his major league debut. The 24-year-old received a raucous standing ovation from the Camden Yards crowd as he took the field, and few could forget the indelible image of Rutschman doing a 360 to soak in the atmosphere before donning his mask, giving a slight nod as if to say, "Yeah, I belong here."

Rutschman brought the kind of pedigree that few O's rookies could ever match. He was a former #1 draft pick, only the second in Orioles history, and was the top-ranked prospect in baseball as he destroyed minor league pitching all the way up the ladder. In an O's minor league system that had been replenished with young talent since the hiring of Mike Elias in 2018, Rutschman was the leader of the pack, the franchise cornerstone who would usher in an era of perennially contending Orioles teams. The future of Baltimore baseball was incredibly bright.

Now look at us. Four years later, the Orioles still haven't won a postseason game in the Elias era. And Rutschman, the linchpin of the Birds' expected renaissance, is gone, traded away to a division rival while he was on the injured list. All that's left in Birdland is a big old mess.

It's safe to say that the Adley Rutschman Experience in Baltimore didn't turn out as anyone expected. Which is not to say he was a bust. In fact, the first three years of his career could hardly have been more successful in terms of his on-field production. Adley racked up 12.9 bWAR from 2022-24, the third-most in Orioles history for a player in his first three seasons (behind Gunnar Henderson's 15.8 and Nick Markakis' 14.0). Rutschman was AL Rookie of the Year runner-up in 2022, and collected a Silver Slugger award, two All-Star selections, and two top-12 AL MVP finishes in that three-year span.

You could make a legitimate case that Adley was the best catcher in baseball at the time, or at least the one with the brightest career in front of him. And his arrival did, indeed, usher in an era of homegrown O's prospects who brought postseason baseball back to Baltimore for two years, including a 103-win season and an AL East crown in 2023. But in both seasons, the Birds were swept out of the postseason.

As Orioles fans are all too painfully aware, though, Rutschman's career — and the Orioles' fortunes — took a nosedive starting in mid-2024. From June 22 to the end of the season, Rutschman batted a horrendous .192 with a .574 OPS in 77 games as the O's limped into the playoffs. A prevailing theory among O's fans is that Adley was battling a secret injury during that time, though Rutschman never admitted as much. Distressingly, his 2025 was even worse: oblique strains in both his legs landed him on the IL twice, and in 90 games he batted just .220/.307/.366 with nine home runs, a major reason why the Orioles collapsed to a last-place finish.

Rutschman entered the 2026 season with something to prove. A few things, actually. He needed to prove he could still hit like the Adley of 2022-23. He needed to prove he was still the Orioles' go-to catcher even after the O's committed an eight-year contract to Samuel Basallo in 2025. And he needed to prove he could still be the bedrock of the Birds' return to contention.

Rutschman was unsuccessful on the last of those points and only somewhat so on the other two. He played the lion's share behind the plate while he was on the team, starting 49 of the Orioles' first 98 games. And his bat was the best it's been in three years. He posted a 116 OPS+ for the Birds, batting .251 with a .764 OPS, sparking gleeful cries of "Adley is so back!" from O's fans who'd been long awaiting his return to form. His defense, too, was vastly improved over the past couple of years, particularly when throwing out basestealers. Rutschman's 33.9 CS% was the best mark of his career and far outpaced the MLB average of 22.7. He led all AL catchers with 21 caught stealings.

Adley's early-season heroics earned him his third career All-Star selection, serving as the Orioles' lone representative at the Midsummer Classic in Philadelphia on July 14. It turned out to be his third-to-last game in an O's uniform. During the Birds' series in Houston to start the second half, Rutschman suffered left wrist inflammation that landed him on the 10-day IL — and, though we didn't know it at the time, wrapped up his Orioles career.

As the O's continued to wallow in mediocrity at the Aug. 3 trade deadline, Rutschman's name was bandied about as a trade candidate. Logically it made sense, due to the Orioles' commitment to Basallo and Adley's 1.5 years until free agency, but still it came as a shock to much of Birdland when Elias actually pulled the trigger on a deal. Especially shocking is that the O's traded him to division rival Boston, of all places, for Carlos Narváez and four prospects.

And just like that, it was over. Adley Rutschman, the one-time face of the franchise, was unceremoniously jettisoned by the Birds while on the injured list, leaving so much unfinished business with the team he was supposed to lead to the promised land. He'll always be remembered fondly by most O's fans, and his up-and-down five-year Orioles career brought more highlights than lowlights. Ultimately, though, Adley Rutschman never quite lived up to the inordinate hype that accompanied him. And the Orioles' early success after his arrival in the majors didn't last.

The return package for Rutschman, which featured top Red Sox pitching prospect Anthony Eyanson and several other highly-regarded youngsters, was widely praised. Still, to see a much-ballyhooed #1 draft pick come and go from Baltimore without the O's ever winning even one playoff game is a rather damning indictment of Elias's vision for the organization, and if I were the owner of the team he'd have gotten his pink slip some time ago. But David Rubenstein doesn't see it that way, and so Elias remains, albeit with a heavily restructured front office. Perhaps someday the Orioles will finally find that cornerstone player who can return to the franchise to championship glory.

As for Rutschman, he's surely got more years ahead of him to torment the Orioles, as he did in his return to Camden Yards with the Red Sox on Sept. 3 when he smacked two home runs to beat the Birds. He'll be under contract with Boston for 2027 before reaching free agency at age 30, and I'll be fascinated to see what kind of contract he gets. How much will teams be willing to pay for an aging catcher whose offense has fluctuated wildly from year to year?

It's strange to think that the Orioles will open the 2027 season without Rutschman behind the plate for the first time in five years. And it's frustrating that his tenure with the Birds didn't pan out like we'd dreamed of. But thanks for the memories all the same, Adley.

#2865. Knicks enjoy history-tying 84-point first half in dominant win

The Knicks broke out of their early-game slump in historic fashion.

They erupted for 84 points in the first half of their 135-105 rout of the Bulls on Wednesday night at Madison Square Garden. It tied a franchise record set on Nov. 18, 1988, against the 76ers.

But the Knicks actually lost that game, 137-135.

Wednesday, on the other hand, represented the Knicks' best and by far most complete showing of the season.

Jalen Brunson celebrates after hitting a 3-pointer during the Knicks' 135-105 blowout win over the Bulls on Nov. 4, 2026 at Madison Square Garden. Charles Wenzelberg / New York Post

The 84 points were also the most the Knicks have ever scored in any half at the current Madison Square Garden.

"I really liked how we started out," coach Mike Brown said. "Spacing the floor well, touching the paint, and then re-spacing too. Our re-spacing was really quick and really decisive. We had some great, great looks early on. And everybody played well offensively.

"Our pace was pretty good, it's something we've been talking about. Our offensive rebounding, for shooting a high percentage, was pretty good. Just a lot of good things."

Entering Wednesday, the Knicks were averaging just 51.6 points in first halves — the third-worst mark in the NBA and better than only the Bucks and Nets. They were shooting a paltry 39.2 percent from the field in first halves — worst in the NBA.

OG Anunoby goes up for a layup during the Knicks' win over the Bulls. Charles Wenzelberg / New York Post

It led to constant deficits they had to fight back from.

But they shot 62.5 percent (25-for-40) from the field and 50 percent (10-for-20) from 3-point range during Wednesday's first half and led by 32 at the break.

Jalen Brunson had 26 of those 84 first-half points, going a red-hot 8-for-11 from the field and 4-for-6 from 3-point range. OG Anunoby added 18 first-half points.

"Obviously, making 3s, but I think making our two-pointers are really important as well," Brunson said. "… When you have it going, it feels good. Just trying to play off that and use your gravity to make plays. I feel like it really started on the defensive side of the ball, we were able to get stops and get out in transition."

It also helped that the Knicks took a staggering 26 free throws in the first half — making 24 of them. Anunoby was 11-for-12 from the line in the first half, relentlessly attacking the rim.

The Bulls took just six first-half free throws, making five.

The historic start allowed for plenty of late-game rest at a time the Knicks have talked about dealing with physical fatigue given their short offseason. All five starters sat the entire fourth quarter.

A nice luxury thanks to an electric start.

"It was a really good half," Brown said, "in terms of doing what we believe we should be doing offensively as our staples. Everybody was really good in those areas."

#2864. Fantasy football Start ‘Em, Sit ‘Em: 30 players to start or sit in Week 9

Week 9 of the 2026 NFL season has already brought with it plenty of chaos, as several teams are making notable moves at the quarterback position.

A microcosm of the league's greater movement can be seen with the Baltimore Ravens. The Ravens lost Lamar Jackson and Tyler Huntley to long-term injuries and will start undrafted rookie Joe Fagnano on "Thursday Night Football." However, they are also planning to trade for Arizona Cardinals quarterback Jacoby Brissett over the weekend, so their quarterback room is in flux.

The same is true with the Seattle Seahawks, where Drew Lock will replace an injured Sam Darnold, and with the Cleveland Browns, where Shedeur Sanders may start with Deshaun Watson in concussion protocol. And that's not to mention the Philadelphia Eagles' decision to bench Tanner McKee to see what they have in the potential-packed Joe Milton.

That swath of quarterback changes will leave many fantasy managers with difficult start 'em, sit 'em decisions. Those quandaries will also exist at other positions like running back, where fantasy footballers will have to decide whether to trust Ashton Jeanty or Tyler Allgeier, among others.

Who can you start and sit in fantasy football for Week 9 of the 2026 NFL season? USA TODAY Sports outlines 30 players to start or sit.

Malik Willis, Miami Dolphins (vs. Detroit Lions)

Willis is starting to round into form for the Dolphins and has scored multiple touchdowns in three consecutive games. During that span, he has averaged 37.7 rushing yards per game, which will raise his floor in most matchups. The Lions have allowed the most fantasy points per game (FPPG) to quarterbacks this season, so Willis should be positioned to have a strong showing in what figures to be a favorable, high-scoring matchup.

Drew Lock, Seattle Seahawks (vs. Arizona Cardinals)

The Cardinals are one of just three NFL teams to allow 18 passing touchdowns to quarterbacks this season, along with the Lions and the Las Vegas Raiders. Unsurprisingly, Arizona has allowed a league-high 29.8 fantasy points per game to the position because of that, so Lock should be positioned for a nice outing in which he could toss multiple touchdowns.

Joe Milton, Philadelphia Eagles (vs. New York Giants)

If you're looking for a fun dart throw, Milton could be worth considering. He's set to start in place of Tanner McKee and has the cannon arm and elite athleticism needed to blossom into a fantasy asset. The Giants have allowed the seventh-most FPPG to quarterbacks, so Milton has a chance to emerge as a decent streamer.

Quinshon Judkins, Cleveland Browns (at New Orleans Saints)

Judkins has been boom-or-bust as a touchdown-dependent fantasy option, but he should be poised for a good outing against the Saints. New Orleans has allowed the most FPPG to running backs this season, including a league-high 11 rushing touchdowns to the position. With that in mind, Judkins should be able to find his way into the end zone.

Jonah Coleman, Denver Broncos (at Carolina Panthers)

Coleman took on a lion's share of Denver's backfield touches in Week 9, posting 104 total yards and a touchdown on 15 touches (11 carries, four receptions). The rookie should continue in that role and has a great matchup against a Panthers defense that has allowed the second-most FPPG to running backs this season.

Tyler Allgeier, Arizona Cardinals (at Seattle Seahawks)

Seattle is a tough matchup for any running back, but Allgeier figures to get great volume with Jeremiyah Love (ankle) on IR and Bam Knight dealing with a concussion. That could be enough to make him a touchdown-dependent flex play after he popped off for 191 total yards and two touchdowns against the Cowboys.

Jadarian Price, Seattle Seahawks (vs. Arizona Cardinals)

Price and Zach Charbonnet split carries for the Seahawks against the Bears. Neither was particularly effective but each gets a much easier matchup in Week 9 against a Cardinals defense that has been middle-of-the-pack against running backs this season. Price has some explosiveness, so don't be surprised if this is his breakout game.

Caleb Douglas, Miami Dolphins (vs. Detroit Lions)

As mentioned, the Lions have been weak against the pass this year. If we're recommending to start Willis, then Douglas should get a nod too, as the rookie has notched six receptions for 113 yards and two touchdowns in two games since returning from an early-season ankle injury.

Ladd McConkey, Los Angeles Chargers (vs. Houston Texans)

Trusting McConkey may seem risky, given that Justin Herbert has struggled under pressure this season. That said, the Texans are allowing the second-most FPPG to receivers this season and McConkey is fresh off a four-catch, 86-yard outing that was one of his best of the season. He should be in line for a solid showing against the Texans.

Josh Downs, Indianapolis Colts (vs. Dallas Cowboys)

Could this be a showcase game for Downs ahead of the 2026 NFL trade deadline? It sure feels like it. Dallas has allowed the fifth-most FPPG to receivers this season, and the Colts may be eager to boost Downs' trade value by targeting him early and often in this spot.

Brian Thomas Jr., Jacksonville Jaguars (at Baltimore Ravens)

The same is true of Thomas, who could be traded as he sees his role shrink in Jacksonville. He caught a touchdown last week and could be in line for ample playing time if the Jaguars can build a big lead against a Joe Fagnano-led Ravens team on "Thursday Night Football."

Mike Gesicki, Cincinnati Bengals (at Atlanta Falcons)

Gesicki has scored in five consecutive games and six of the seven he has played this season. Joe Burrow has thrown 13 touchdown passes over his last three games, so Gesicki should continue to have high touchdown upside regardless of his opponent.

Greg Dulcich, Miami Dolphins (vs. Detroit Lions)

Dulcich has posted at least four catches and 37 yards in four of his last five games. Now, he gets to face a Lions defense that is allowing the most receptions (61), receiving yards (684) and receiving touchdowns (11) to tight ends this season. He could emerge as a surprise top-10 tight end this week.

Jacksonville Jaguars (at Baltimore Ravens)

The Jaguars are playing the Ravens on a short week. Baltimore is expected to start third-string quarterback Joe Fagnano, an undrafted rookie, after injuries to Lamar Jackson and Tyler Huntley. Fagnano completed 10 of 21 passes for 91 yards and an interception while being sacked three times against the Bills. The Jaguars should pressure him into numerous mistakes while their top-ranked run defense should be able to bottle up Derrick Henry.

The Lions will likely give up some yardage and points to the Dolphins, but they should also generate plenty of sacks. Detroit has 24 sacks this season, third-most in the NFL, while Malik Willis has been sacked 21 times through seven starts.

Bryce Young, Carolina Panthers (vs. Denver Broncos)

Young has regressed over the last two weeks after a torrid start to the season, completing just 54.4% of his passes for 372 yards, two touchdowns and three interceptions during Carolina's two-game losing skid. The main issue? Young has been pressured a lot in those contests, and he has just a 64 passer rating when pressured compared to 106.3 when kept clean, per Pro Football Focus. The Broncos rank fourth in pressure rate league-wide, per the NFL's Next Gen Stats, so they should be able to limit Young in this favorable spot.

Bo Nix, Denver Broncos (at Carolina Panthers)

The Panthers have a banged-up secondary, but it still won't be easy to justify starting Nix. The Broncos quarterback has looked better recently, throwing for exactly 222 yards in back-to-back games and scoring twice in each. Still, the Panthers are typically more susceptible against the run, so Nix has a lower ceiling than most streaming options this week.

Daniel Jones, Indianapolis Colts (vs. Dallas Cowboys)

Normally, the quarterback playing the Cowboys is a solid streaming option. However, with Jones facing down the potential for a benching and having failed to throw multiple touchdown passes in a game this season, it's best to steer clear of him.

Ashton Jeanty, Las Vegas Raiders (at San Francisco 49ers)

Can you really trust Jeanty after the Raiders gave him just two carries against the Jets while giving Mike Washington Jr. a whopping 25? Jeanty will remain productive as a receiver, but his uncertain between-the-tackles workload makes it hard to trust the former first-round pick, especially against a 49ers defense allowing just 3.6 yards per carry to running backs this season. It's better to wait and see whether Jeanty's decrease in carries was punishment for trash-talking the Jets before Week 8 or a sign of what's to come in Klint Kubiak's running back rotation.

Breece Hall, New York Jets (at Kansas City Chiefs)

Hall seems likely to return from a nagging quad injury this week, but he gets a tough matchup against a Chiefs defense that has largely bottled up opposing running backs this season. Hall may also be splitting carries with Braelon Allen, who has thrived in his stead, so this doesn't seem like an ideal spot to trust him.

Aaron Jones and Jordan Mason, Minnesota Vikings (at Buffalo Bills)

We'll do two for the price of one here. The Vikings have a bottom-six rushing offense this season in terms of EPA per play, per the NFL's Next Gen Stats. Jones and Mason are also stuck in a frustrating time share, so neither seems like a particularly viable play against a Bills defense that has allowed just 97.4 rushing yards per game this season.

Michael Wilson, Arizona Cardinals (at Seattle Seahawks)

Wilson finally had a breakout game for the first time since Marvin Harrison Jr. was traded, generating eight catches for 111 yards and a touchdown against the Cowboys. He'll have a much tougher matchup against a Seahawks team that has been excellent against receivers this year, especially after Wilson suffered a couple of broken ribs on his touchdown catch.

Adonai Mitchell, New York Jets (at Kansas City Chiefs)

Mitchell just logged seven catches for 142 yards and a touchdown against the Raiders in Week 8. He gets a much tougher matchup in Week 9 against a Chiefs defense that has allowed the second-fewest FPPG to receivers this season. Add in that Omar Cooper Jr. could also siphon targets from him and Mitchell may be a hit-or-miss play each week even if Garrett Wilson (concussion) is unable to play.

Jalen Coker, Carolina Panthers (vs. Denver Broncos)

The Broncos get a lot of pressure, so Young won't have much time to throw in that matchup. That could limit Coker's deep-ball upside, and while he could rack up yards after the catch, it's hard to trust him to do so against a quality defense.

Khalil Shakir, Buffalo Bills (at Minnesota Vikings)

Shakir started well in the Bills' win over the Ravens but did little outside the first drive. DJ Moore seems likely to continue getting most of the attention from Josh Allen, so don't be surprised if Shakir struggles against a Vikings defense that has allowed the third-fewest FPPG to receivers this season.

Dalton Kincaid, Buffalo Bills (at Minnesota Vikings)

Kincaid scored a touchdown last week for the first time since Week 2, but he will be hard-pressed to repeat that feat against the Vikings. Minnesota has yet to allow a receiving touchdown to tight ends this season, so Kincaid figures to be limited.

T.J. Hockenson, Minnesota Vikings (vs. Buffalo Bills)

The Bills have only allowed one touchdown to tight ends this season. It also isn't clear whether Kyler Murray (hamstring) will play in this contest, so Hockenson might have a lower ceiling in this matchup than most.

No NFL team has allowed fewer points per game than the Vikings (13.3). No NFL team has scored more points per game than the Bills (33.3). Something will give in this matchup, but if there's one quarterback that's built to beat Brian Flores' pressure-happy scheme, it's Josh Allen.

San Francisco 49ers (vs. Las Vegas Raiders)

The 49ers are favored to beat the Raiders, but this could end up being a shootout given how Kirk Cousins and Co. have been playing. Las Vegas is averaging 27.6 points per game, so even if Nick Bosa returns, this is still a low-floor spot for San Francisco.

#2863. Miami Hurricanes Football: 3 players who need to step up in Malachi Toney’s absence

On Wednesday, reports broke that Miami Hurricanes star WR Malachi Toney sustained an ankle injury in practice. Later reports indicated that Toney will have surgery to fix the injury, and miss 4-6 weeks to recover. Our piece on these reports can be found here:

While the injury is a tough one to deal with, and we wish Toney a safe surgery and complete recovery, the season continues. Miami travels to South Bend to face off against Notre Dame this week, and has 3 more ACC games after that as well.

So, while there isn't any player who can fully replace Toney, here are 3 players who need to step up their performance and production to keep Miami's offense performing as one of the best in America:

The other big transfer from Duke, Barkate leads the list of players who can, and needs to, step up his performance and impact.

A 6'1" 195lb receiver, Barkate has a long history of elite performance at the college level. After starring at Harvard for 3 years, Barkate transferred to Duke last year. While there, he partnered with QB Darian Mensah (ever heard of him?) and put up a 2nd team All-ACC season. 72 catches for 1,106 yards and 7 touchdowns. Huge numbers for the ACC Champions as the clear #1 target.

With Toney out, Barkate now returns to his spot as Mensah's #1 option. He's a dynamic receiver who can carry the load for a top offense. He's been very good as the #2 option for Miami this year, and posted solid stats with 28 catches for 372 yards and 4 touchdowns. He's the easy and right choice for the player mostly likely, and most able, to step into the spotlight as the focal point of Miami's passing attack moving forward.

Someone that was billed as "the best and most athletic player on the roster", Lofton is finally healthy for the first time in a couple of seasons and he's flashing the kind of talent that earned him that high praise. I mean, just look at this picture, and the hurdle from the Carolina game, and you see the athleticism and playmaking that made him a blue chip recruit, and the starting TE on this roster.

Lofton is a multifaceted playmaker for the Canes offense. He works well in the RPO game as a flat and seam receiver. He's good in the screen game as a receiver and blocker. And he's great in space and after the catch (see the picture and video above), and he's a mismatch for opposing defenses to contend with. His 20 catches for 236 yards and 2 touchdowns rank 4th on the Canes this year, but he is a prime option to do a lot of the between-the-numbers receiving work that Toney did, but with his own spin.

I couldn't decide which other receiver to put here…so I'm putting both. Fight me.

Wingo and Jacobs bring different skillsets and abilities to the field, and each can find a role in the revamped Miami offense.

A blue chip true freshman, Wingo has a combination of size, speed, and skill that Miami should be keen to leverage. He's worked his way into more playing time both as a kick returner and receiver as the year has progressed, and now there's nothing but opportunity for him to make an even larger impact for this team. Wingo has 8 catches for 142 yards and a touchdown so far, but the sky is the limit for him.

#2860. Diving deeper into Cavs 124-116 loss to Thunder: Cavaliers are too reliant on James Harden

It was another day in the office for the reigning back-to-back MVP. SGA got to his spots on the floor, no matter how many defenders they threw his way. This allowed him to score over 40 points for the second time this week against the Cavs.

There was simply nothing Cleveland could do to slow down Gilgeous-Alexander, or really, even make it challenging.

Ajay Mitchell provided timely baskets whenever it seemed like the Cavs were getting any kind of momentum. He served as the offensive engine when SGA was off the court, and as the counterpunch when he was.

27 points on 10-of-17 shooting, 6 assists, 3 rebounds, 1 steal

Mitchell's stat line is a little deceiving. He was an incredibly efficient scorer, but he didn't make a constant impact throughout all four quarters.

Anything bought from the links helps support Fear the Sword. You can buy the Browns throwback shirt HERE. You can also shop all of Homage's Cleveland gear HERE.

9 points, 0 assists, 1 rebound, 2 turnovers, 6 fouls

Thomas looked like a rookie for one of the first times this season. He struggled to make an impact on the scoreboard and was picked on defensively — particularly by the reigning MVP when he got an opportunity to do so. This led to Thomas fouling out in just 18 minutes.

12 points on 5-for-10 shooting, 8 rebounds

The Cavs need someone to provide tertiary ball-handling, rebounding, and who thinks the game at a high level. Hezonja has consistently supplied that and did so again in Oklahoma City.

I'm not sure why Hezonja doesn't get more minutes than he does, or see the floor in closing situations — especially in a game Jarrett Allen left with an injury. In this one, head coach Kenny Atkinson went with Tyrese Proctor (until he left with an injury) and then with Craig Porter Jr. Having a third guard makes sense for a team that struggles with ball pressure, but can't Hezonja help with that in addition to supplying extra rebounding and shooting? I just don't get it.

Proctor performed well in his second career start. He provided some off-ball shooting and held his own defensively. That's what you want to see from a second-year player who's thrown into the starting lineup.

An injury to Allen forced Enaruna into his first-ever rotation minutes, and he performed admirably. His size and energy on the defensive end were much needed on an evening the Cavs were severely lacking wing defenders due to injuries — even if he wasn't necessarily perfect on that end.

The offensive numbers weren't necessarily impressive. Enaruna went just 2-for-7 from the field, which included going 0-for-3 from distance. However, a couple of those threes went halfway down before popping back out.

Getting serviceable minutes from two-way players is more necessary than ever. Pace, offensive rebounding, and where defenders are picking up their offensive assignments are higher than ever. This has created more injuries. Throw in the second-apron restrictions, and it's almost a necessity for teams to have two-way players (whose salaries don't count against the cap) that can provide fill-in rotation minutes when needed.

This performance doesn't mean Enaruna will be a mainstay in the rotation or anything like that, but it did show that he can provide playable minutes when called upon.

Mitchell was awesome down the stretch, it just came too little too late.

"Dissapointed in our first quarter. Three quarers [were] really solid play, and you have one quarter where you're not up to par. Like I said, the turnoves, the live-ball turnovers, they just get the other team going, and you know, it kind of snow balls."

The Cavs have struggled to stop the bleeding so far this year. There's been one quarter, or extended stretch of play in each of their losses where they let go of the rope. That happened in the first quarter here, when they were beaten 37-20. Cleveland outscored Oklahoma City for each of the next three quarters, but that doesn't matter much when you have a start like this.

Only 20 of Cleveland's 93 shots came at the rim (16th percentile).

The Cavs' three-point volume and accuracy allowed them to have a slightly above league-average offensive output in this game. However, it's nearly impossible to have a truly effective offense if you aren't getting to the rim well. If you aren't getting to the basket, you likely aren't getting to the line either, which was an issue for the Cavs.

This game turned around when Harden did. There was a stretch from the end of the second quarter to the start of the third where Harden looked like the best version of himself for one of the few times this season.

Harden was up to his old tricks during that run. He was able to establish the three-point shot midway through the second quarter, which opened up the rest of his game. The threat of that shot caused defenders to bite too hard on step-backs and made them a step slow when he drove inside. This allowed Harden to be an effective playmaker at all three levels, which isn't something he's been able to do on command so far this campaign. He scored or assisted on 16 points during the Cavs' 18-3 run at the start of the third quarter that allowed Cleveland to make this a moderately competitive game.

The Cavs' success this year hinges on Harden's, which is why things have been so rocky at the start. Harden has posted his career-worst free-throw rate and has struggled to hit anything inside 14 feet. This has handicapped his effectiveness and left him mostly an outside shooter.

Cleveland desperately needs the version of Harden we got a glimpse of here if they want to succeed against high-level teams. Or at the very least, they need that iteration if they're going to be this isolation-heavy with both guards.

The entire offense is predicated on the guards drawing extra defenders to them. If they can do that, the kick-out threes open up, as do windows to get their bigs involved. Conversely, when they aren't getting inside, the ball and player movement can stagnate. This leads to turnovers and settling for contested jump shots — as we've seen during Cleveland's worst stretches.

Relying this heavily on a 37-year-old isn't ideal, but it's where the Cavs find themselves. And they will continue to be at this spot unless they drastically alter their offensive process.

#2854. Four Takeaways from the Raptors’ 128-109 loss to Nuggets

The Toronto Raptors continue an up-and-down start to the season without Kawhi Leonard after losing 128-109 to the Denver Nuggets on Wednesday.

With the loss, Toronto falls to 4-4 on the season and 2-4 without Leonard.

Toronto is a poor three-point shooting team. Entering the contest, the Raptors averaged 31.5 per cent from beyond the arc, which ranks 27th in the NBA.

While the perimeter shooting couldn't sustain itself (Toronto finished at 35 per cent), the opening quarter featured a Raptors team that felt dangerous from three. Toronto went an impressive 6-for-12 from the arc. For context, the Raptors averaged 11.5 triples per game.

The opening 12 minutes were a breath of fresh air, especially after the team's abysmal 8-for-29 performance against the Los Angeles Clippers. This season, the league average from three is currently at 34.8 per cent. Toronto has shot better than 34.8 per cent three times in eight games.

Unfortunately, the Raptors shot 6-for-22 the rest of the way.

It should be made clear: tonight's loss was not on Immanuel Quickley.

But it was pointed out on the TSN broadcast that Quickley needs to have a consistent impact through all four quarters. Quickley was brilliant in the opening 12 minutes, finishing with 10 points and six assists while shooting 50 per cent from three. He also added two steals.

By the end of the game, Quickly finished with 13 points and seven assists. The point guard also shot 25 per cent from the perimeter and didn't record another steal.

While we suggested that the Raptors could overwhelm Nikola Jokic and the Nuggets, specifically by leveraging their strengths on the offensive glass, it turns out that the game goes well beyond the battle of the boards. The future Hall of Famer finished with 30 points, 10 rebounds and 11 assists while pummelling the Raptors into submission.

Jokic emerged from halftime ready to shift into another gear. While in the Denver air, Toronto didn't stand a chance. Jokic had already safely recorded his triple-double by the end of the third quarter. In the same period, he tied the entire Raptors team in points with 15.

Referencing the Colorado air might also be doing Jokic a disservice. The big man was ultimately responsible for 26 of the Nuggets' 33 points in the first quarter.

The Nuggets had limited the Raptors to seven fast-break points with just over three minutes remaining in the third quarter. Stopping Toronto in transition was likely a focal point for Denver head coach David Adelman and his staff. The Raptors entered the game second in transition points at 19.7 per game.

For the Raptors to salvage their four-game road trip, they'll need to either get back to what they do best on the breaks or find ways to score in the half-court. Their next opponent, the Milwaukee Bucks, is 11th in fastbreak points allowed per game at 13.3

#2853. WWE Crown Jewel 2026 will be remembered for all the wrong reasons

On paper, it should be a must-see match: Roman Reigns vs. Sami Zayn. The last time these contrasting rivals went head-to-head in the ring back in February 2023, it ended up being the high point of the entire Bloodline saga — an extremely juicy cherry on top of an already delicious cake.

Now, Reigns vs. Zayn are set to do battle again, for only the second time in history, at this weekend's WWE Crown Jewel. And our excitement levels? Well, they're not exactly through the roof. For whatever happens in the squared circle come Saturday afternoon, it almost certainly won't be what we remember most about this most controversial of PLEs.

Instead, this year's Crown Jewel is set to be remembered for one thing only: WWE's decision to stick to its original plans to run an event in Saudi Arabia during what looks a hell of a lot like an ongoing conflict involving what the U.S. government considers to be an active terrorist organization, namely the Iran-backed Houthis.

That has been the story over the past month, as we've watched in disbelief as WWE has stuck by its Saudi plans (first announced in August. when things looked much more peaceful). Every time we figured they would change course — not just after the lethal strikes on Riyadh airport in early October, but also after the U.S. government opted to evacuate some diplomats from the city — we were left in the same position, waiting for the news that never arrived.

So now here we are: Less than 48 hours away from what could well be the most ill-advised pro-wrestling event since Antonio Inoki and Eric Bischoff were duped into organizing a propaganda spectacle for the North Korean government back in 1995. Travel advisories and terrorist threats be damned: WWE is heading to Riyadh.

Roman Reigns vs. Sami Zayn is happening this weekend in Saudi Arabia come hell or high water.

Obviously, we hope the event goes as smoothly as possible. Realistically, it almost certainly will — just as last week's Saul "Canelo" Alvarez fight passed without incident too. But that doesn't mean that this year's Crown Jewel isn't going to leave a lasting stain on WWE's corporate image, and that of its parent company TKO.

Just look at some of the things we've seen over the past few weeks. The fact that Ari Emanuel, the all-powerful head of the TKO empire, was grilled about the wisdom of the decision to go to Saudi Arabia during what was supposed to be a softball interview with Fox News's Bret Baier. That's the sort of thing that tends to stick around — and not just in the wrestling press.

Then there was the leaked audio from TKO's international town-hall meeting, obtained by POST Wrestling. For weeks, we've heard whispers of talent and staffers being worried about working a Saudi show in the circumstances. Now here was confirmation of that discontent, coming straight from the mouth of Mark Shapiro, one of the top names in the TKO hierarchy.

"We're all hoping and praying everything goes off without a hitch," said Shapiro, TKO's Chief Operating Officer, speaking over video conference to invited WWE talent and staffers. He went on to thank all those staff who have worked on the ground at events across the wider Middle East region while assuring his audience that, despite appearances, WWE wouldn't hesitate to postpone Crown Jewel should there be "further escalation."

Had Shapiro been the one in the Fox hot seat, Bret Baier might have asked him exactly what sort of escalation he was waiting for, given that the U.S. Embassy in Riyadh issued a fresh warning about bubbling tensions just this week. Though I appreciate that the scope for adversarial questions is slightly thinner when it comes to internal staff meetings.

Mark Shapiro, seen here next to Paul Levesque, recently led a leaked TKO town hall over Saudi concerns.

Even so, a C-suite executive having to reassure staffers that the company doesn't want to send them into an actual warzone? That's the sort of thing that can have a long shelf life. It also makes me even more convinced that this year's Crown Jewel, or at least its build-up, will end up joining the ranks of historic controversies that have dogged the whole WWE-Saudi Arabia relationship for the past decade.

I'm talking here about things like WWE having to run all-male cards for its initial Crown Jewel shows. Or the ongoing fascination about why WWE's charter jet was held on the tarmac back in 2019. Or the bizarre moment ahead of last year's Night of Champions when CM Punk ended up offering an on-stage apology for his previous disparaging comments about the country.

Individually, those incidents were never going to sink this relationship on their own. But added together they contribute to that feeling — the one that WWE so hard to shake over the past decade — that there's just something murky about this whole Saudi relationship.

It's almost enough to make you feel sorry for Roman Reigns, Cody Rhodes, Chelsea Green, Liv Morgan and all the other performers who will be tasked with putting on a pro-wrestling show amid the circumstances. I mean, just compare the vibes around this event to the last time that Roman Reigns took on Sami Zayn, back in that aforementioned title match at the peak of the Bloodline saga.

What did we have back then? A hot-as-hell crowd in Montreal. A groundswell of support for the creative direction. A feeling that, for all the inherent cliches in pro-wrestling, WWE was actually building to something special. If anyone had mentioned safety concerns, you'd have guessed they were talking about the chances of Roman Reigns, then the hottest heel in pro-wrestling, leaving the Bell Center in one piece.

That Reigns and Zayn delivered a five-star match was the perfect end to that chapter. So what would happen if they were to repeat that achievement this Saturday afternoon? Sure, it might create a bit of buzz across social media on Saturday night and some highlight packages for "Raw" on Monday. But would it really change how any of us look back on this event in a year's time? Would it make this whole fiasco look any smarter?

On that front, you have to feel the damage is done — regardless of whatever Ari Emanuel and Mark Shapiro might tell you.

#2852. Why isn't Lamar Jackson playing today? Injury update, return timeline for Ravens QB

The Baltimore Ravens are taking on the Jacksonville Jaguars in a "Thursday Night Football" game that could prove crucial for their chances of staying in the AFC North race.

The Ravens will have to navigate that game, and the foreseeable future, without the services of their starting quarterback, Lamar Jackson.

Jackson suffered a thumb injury that is expected to sideline him long-term. This marks the second time this season the veteran quarterback is facing a multi-game absence, after missing three games leading up to Baltimore's Week 8 game against the Buffalo Bills with an ankle injury.

Here's everything you need to know about Jackson's thumb injury and when he might return to the field.

Jackson suffered a thumb injury in the Ravens' Week 8 loss to the Buffalo Bills.

The injury occurred on Jackson's first passing attempt of the game, when he hit his throwing hand on the arm of Bills pass rusher Gregory Rousseau. Jackson immediately reached for his hand in pain and was seen clutching it while running toward the sideline.

Jackson was quickly deemed out for the remainder of the game. He was later spotted wearing a cast on his injured hand after he returned to the field clad in street clothes during the second half of the contest.

Before the game against Buffalo, Jackson had missed the previous three games because of an ankle injury. He has appeared in five of the Ravens' eight games this season but has only finished three.

The Ravens have not provided a definitive timeline for Jackson's return, but coach Jesse Minter confirmed the star quarterback will be placed on IR because of his thumb injury.

"That'll be a surgery deal," Minter said when discussing Jackson's injury during a postgame news conference on Sunday, Nov. 1. "He'll go to IR. That's a tough deal."

Players placed on IR must miss a minimum of four games, per NFL rules. That would guarantee Jackson misses the Ravens' Weeks 9-12 games before becoming eligible to return for their Week 14 contest against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, which comes after their Week 13 bye.

But Minter did acknowledge that Jackson's injury could "potentially" be season-ending. He also declined to provide updates about the quarterback's thumb when asked during a Monday, Nov. 2 news conference.

"I'm not going to get into the specifics of the injury," Minter told reporters.

Minter did reveal Jackson had not yet had surgery to repair his thumb malady and that the Ravens would likely have a more concrete update about his status "maybe sometime this week."

The Ravens have not yet clarified whether Jackson will be able to return during the 2026 NFL season. Minter simply said the injury was "potentially" season-ending but did not offer a concrete timeline for the veteran quarterback's return.

Normally, veteran Tyler Huntley would take on that mantle in Jackson's absence. However, he is dealing with a turf toe injury and is expected to miss the rest of the season because of it.

That has left third-string quarterback Joe Fagnano to serve as the starter for "Thursday Night Football" in Week 9. The undrafted rookie spent the final three seasons of his college career at UConn and completed 68% of his passes for 3,448 yards, 28 touchdowns and one interception during his sixth and final college season.

Fagnano (6-3, 230 pounds) completed 10 of 21 passes for 91 yards and an interception in relief of Jackson and Huntley against the Bills.

That said, Fagnano isn't expected to be the Ravens' long-term starter. The team has agreed to acquire veteran quarterback Jacoby Brissett in a trade with the Arizona Cardinals, and Brissett will assume the starting mantle beginning in Week 10, if all goes well.

Brissett has previous experience working with Ravens quarterback coach Israel Woolfork during their time together with the Arizona Cardinals.

Baltimore's quarterback depth chart remains in flux with Jackson and Huntley out and Brissett not yet officially acquired.

Brissett is expected to top the Ravens' quarterback depth chart once he officially joins the team, but below is a look at the pecking order within the group for Thursday's game.

Reed signed to the Ravens' practice squad on Monday, Nov. 2, just after Jackson and Huntley's injury. The 2024 undrafted free agent previously played for the Chicago Bears but has never appeared in NFL regular-season game. The Western Kentucky product thrived for the Dallas Renegades during the 2026 UFL season, completing 56.3% of his passes for 1,923 yards, a league-high 21 touchdowns and nine interceptions.

Slovis is another player who went undrafted in 2024. The USC, Pitt and BYU product spent time with four NFL teams before joining the Ravens from the Packers' practice squad. He dressed for two games with the Arizona Cardinals last season and completed 1 of 2 passes for negative-2 yards.

Because Slovis was on the Packers' practice squad, the Ravens needed to sign him to their 53-man roster to obtain him ahead of Thursday's game. That said, the 25-year-old will likely remain behind Reed given that the latter spent time with Baltimore during the preseason – though Slovis, like Brissett, previously played for Woolfork in Arizona.
