#2850. Tyler Kolek gets backup point guard nod in Knicks’ blowout victory

The Knicks' pecking order at backup point guard is fluid.

It was Tyler Kolek, not Jose Alvarado, who was the first point guard off the bench to replace Jalen Brunson during the second quarter of the Knicks' 135-105 rout of the Bulls on Wednesday night at Madison Square Garden.

Kolek played six minutes in that second quarter as the Knicks increased their lead from 22 points to 29.

And Kolek — not Alvarado — returned in the third quarter as well. Alvarado did not play until garbage time in the fourth quarter.

Kolek filled in well when Alvarado missed four games due to a sprained ankle.

But coach Mike Brown, before Alvarado returned Monday against the Nets, said that he would remain the backup point guard and not be punished in the rotation for being injured.

Now, though, the pendulum has swung back to Kolek.

Tyler Kolek, who had five assists in 11 minutes off the bench, drives past Leonard Miller during the Knicks' 135-105 blowout win over the Bulls on Nov. 4, 2026 at Madison Square Garden. AP

"I said this before, every position coming off the bench is a competition, all the time," Brown said. "Nobody's minutes are set in stone. … Jose had the first opportunity in our last game. And then I gave Tyler an opportunity in the second half [against the Nets] and Tyler played well. So I'm gonna go with Tyler. And if I think I need to make a change because Tyler's not getting it done in my eyes, then I'll go back to Jose."

Kolek did not score — and did not attempt a shot — Wednesday but had five assists and no turnovers. Alvarado missed all four shots he took and had two turnovers.

"Both those guys helped us win at a high level [last year]," Brown said. "Tyler helped us win the NBA Cup against San Antonio in Vegas. And Jose helped us win the Finals. So either one of those guys, we feel, can help us in a lot of good ways at any time so they just have to both stay ready."

A 30-point shellacking paved the way for Dalton Knecht to make his Knicks debut.

"He's a scorer. He's not just a shooter. A lot of people think he's a shooter because he's white," Brown joked. "I said it for you, I hope I don't get in trouble. He can go get it."

Knecht had been playing in the G-League since the Knicks signed him to a two-way deal last month.

Brown said he is "not concerned" when asked about Hart's injury outlook.

Hart missed the team's preseason finale against the Raptors due to right ankle soreness and missed time last year due to the same issue.

#2846. Syracuse basketball: two-point guard look presents promise and predicament

The Syracuse Orange basketball team has two drastically different types of players at point guard.

Gerry McNamara has elected to start 6-foot-5 Garwey Dual, a four-year journeyman on his fourth college basketball destination, at the point guard position. McNamara brings in local talent and 6-foot guard Ryan Moesch as the backup. Together the point guard position represents an experience barbell in Dual the senior and Moesch the freshman. Skillsets are also opposite of each other.

"I think they're both really capable. The thing I like is they're both different," Gerry McNamara said.

Syracuse brought in Dual and his 7-foot wingspan to be a versatile defender up top, capable of guarding multiple positions. He's disruptive with his size and length, defending the first point of attack from the opposing team. Dual is capable of managing the offense and scoring from 15-feet and in, but his jumpshot is still a long way off. His strength is on the defensive side of the ball.

"Garwey is great defensively," McNamara said.

Moesch presents talents on the other end of the floor. Eager to make plays, Moesch rolls out of bed and seemingly begins his mornings initiating the fastbreak. He's a skilled passer, has a good feel for the game and seamlessly sets up shots for teammates. He looks to create off the bounce, has a nice hesitation to his game and is more capable of knocking down outside shots than he's showcased thus far.

Moesch's skillset is the inverse of Dual, who says the diverging capabilities are what make each other better.

"I feel like we help each other, find different ways to complement each other," Dual said. "Like I say, sharpen each other's iron every day."

Dual finished with 7 points, 1 rebound, 2 assists and 1 block in 23 minutes Monday night. Moesch struggled in the season-opener with 0 points on 0-8 shooting.

"I think Ryan played terrible. And he had five assists," McNamara said before exacting his communication. "Terrible for him (that is). For what I expect of him. I think Ryan Moesch… can be one of the best point guards in the country. That's why I'm so hard on him."

Moesch didn't shy away from his performance on Monday, assessing his play with the same degree of harshness as his head coach.

"I think I played awful," Moesch said. "I think I could've played a lot better offensively and defensively, making shots and making the right reads.

"I'm not going to let it affect me. I'm not really trippin'. The next game's Thursday. We gotta win."

Moesch has shown a want-to when it comes to staying in front with his on-ball defense when not gambling on steals in the early season, but figures to be much more challenged on that end. Syracuse can't afford to switch defensively from the point guard position when the Orange match up with larger, more physical teams. It's an exploitable mismatch.

In the preseason, however, Moesch has impacted the game when he's come in. He's had at least five assists in all four of Syracuse's games (exhibitions included).

Dual is still working back to game speed after missing two months this summer with a broken collarbone. He's been back to full-speed at Syracuse's practices for about a month.

In the near-term, Moesch played well in Syracuse's exhibition stretch but struggled in the season-opener. As Dual gets back up to speed, the Orange could use Moesch in the non-conference against low-majors.

Dual's experience should be the difference for the point guard position. Syracuse's game against Indiana this Monday will be his 100th college game. In the opening round of the 2026 NCAA Tournament with McNeese, Dual went for 16 points, 3 rebounds, 6 assists, 1 block, and 1 steal against Vanderbilt.

Syracuse needs him and his size for the McNamara is trying to do defensively. McNamara, a former point guard himself, has high demands from that position.

"I think they're both capable of being really good," McNamara said. "But they need to be really good. We can't just be capable. That position demands that you be really good because I'm going to continue to demand it because I think they're both really good."

#2844. Wolves 117, Rockets 107: The Blue Tsunami in Houston

As soon as the game tipped off, one thing was very clear: This was a completely different level of basketball compared to Monday night's game. Unique matchups (LaMelo Ball on Jabari Smith!), shot-making, and game plan discipline meant that the first half was full of back-and-forth, high-quality hoops.

Ayo Dosunmu was such a blue tsunami in transition that even Steve Kornaki had to pause what he was doing and just say, "Wow".

Dosunmu went a perfect 6/6 at the rim on his way to twelve first-half points. On the other side of the floor, Jonathan Kuminga was fantastic on Amen Thompson, playing a brand of athletic and physical basketball that the Wolves haven't been able to do before against Thompson.

The physicality was of note, as he did get a flagrant one after Sengun's face invaded his personal space. Ultimately, it may have been worth it for the repeated over-the-top crowd reaction to the replay, which was genuinely funny.

And finally, the first half story wouldn't be complete without mentioning Jaylen Clark, the certified stuff doer. He had two steals, two offensive rebounds, and a drawn offensive foul. Luckily for the Rockets, the Wolves decided they wanted to keep the game close by shooting free throws with their opposite hands, hitting on just 5/10 as the teams went into halftime tied.

The good basketball continued into the second half, though the third quarter did leave me with a pressing existential question like: "What exactly is a moving screen?" and "Why don't defensive players just run into the screener and fall down every time?"

Outside of that Marcus Smart-inspired existential crisis, both teams essentially played each other even as they headed into the final quarter with the Rockets up two.

As you can see, the start of the fourth quarter was something!

LaMelo Ball committed three fouls in about 30 seconds and put the Rockets in the bonus. But then goes out and totally redeems himself with eight straight points, part of his twelve-point fourth-quarter effort. The back-and-forth affair continued until Jonathan Kuminga drained two huge threes, which, paired with dive-on-the-floor defense and excellent ball movement on offense, would be enough to push the Wolves over the top for the 117-107 victory in Houston.

Let's just get this one out of the way. If the Wolves had lost this game, this would have been the lament in Timberwolves land. They went 10-for-19 from the line, and missing free throws has absolutely been an epidemic for this team. It didn't cost them the game tonight, but they have way too many good shooters for these 1-2 trips to the line.

+14: Points Off Turnover Advantage for the Wolves

Hello defense! From the get-go, I loved the way the Wolves matched up with the Rockets by putting Ayo on Van Fleet, McDaniels on KD, Kuminga on Amen Thompson (more on this soon), and letting LaMelo guard Jabari Smith Jr, a matchup that would force them out of a lot of their offensive sets if they wanted to take advantage of it. This all led to eighteen turnovers for the Rockets and forced them into hitting a lot of tough shots all night.

HOUSTON, TX – NOVEMBER 4: LaMelo Ball #1 of the Minnesota Timberwolves shoots the ball during the game against the Houston Rockets on November 4, 2026 at the Toyota Center in Houston, Texas. Just when we are all ready to be mad at you for three fouls in thirty seconds, you go out there and totally redeem yourself! LaMelo takes home this award for being fantastic in the fourth quarter. He had the perfect balance of finding his own shot, creating offense for others, and forcing Houston to bring double teams that he broke, and helped lead the Wolves to their first clutch-time victory of the season.

The seven turnovers are a reminder it wasn't perfect, but his +15 team high with 20 points, six assists, and four – count 'em, four – stocks show a player that filled the stat sheet and played winning basketball.

The Straight to Jail Award: Jonathan Kuminga

One of the most encouraging aspects of the first nine games of the season for the Wolves has been Jonathan Kuminga's defense. It's one of those things that, if it stays at this level, could be a difference maker come April. In past seasons, Amen Thompson's elite athleticism has been a matchup issue for the Wolves, but Kuminga was all over him tonight, forcing a 3-for-9 night from the field with three turnovers and a team-worst -11.

Straight to jail for Amen Thompson tonight!

He played 25 minutes!

Rudy Gobert had one of his better defensive games against Sengun, but my goodness he needs to finish better. It is not a good sign that my confidence needle in his ability to finish a contested layup has moved into the tossup range with his ability to make a three

Another solid outing from Joan Beringer! By my count, he's now stacked four-to-give good performances in a row

Trey Lyles is the last player hasn't been mentioned, but he was also solid too! He's becoming a very valuable role player that knows what he does best and stays in that zone.

#2839. Are the Tigers a Contenders or Pretenders? Comparing 2026 to Years Past

On October 22, 2022, LSU Football posted a clip of then-head coach Brian Kelly in the locker room saying, "October is for pretenders. November is for contenders."

Kelly told this to his 6-2 team following a 45-20 win over a seventh-ranked, Lane Kiffin-led Ole Miss. The next game the Tigers played would go down as the biggest win of the Brian Kelly era at LSU. On November 5, in Baton Rouge, Kelly and LSU hosted Alabama for Nick Saban's last game coaching in Death Valley. The contest would head into overtime. The Crimson Tide would score first and kick the extra point to make it 31-24. LSU would score on their first offensive play in overtime on a 25-yard Jayden Daniels read option. Kelly made the call to go for two and the win instead of kicking the extra point. You remember how that went, right? Daniels lined up in the shotgun, ball on the left hash, two receivers split out to the right, one tight end on the left, and Mason Taylor lined up as the H-back on the right side; then Taylor motioned across to the left, then back to the right, then the snap, Taylor drifted toward the pylon as Daniels rolled a few steps to his right and fired one over to Taylor, who fell over the goal line for the successful try.

"It's good! LSU does it! Mason Taylor!" Chris Fowler vociferated over the broadcast.

Whether watching at home or rushing the field, it certainly felt as if LSU had returned to contender status in just the first year under Brian Kelly. It was not to be. Kelly led the Tigers to a late-November loss at Texas A&M before dropping a fourth game of the season in the SEC Championship Game to Georgia.

2023 started the way 2022 did: with a loss to Florida State and the Tigers behind the 8-ball. With a 55-49 loss to Kiffin's Ole Miss, LSU had two losses before November arrived. That would be followed up by one final 42-28 death blow to LSU's playoff hopes at the hands of Nick Saban and Alabama.

With 10-4 and 10-3 records under his belt at LSU, 2024's hopes were that Kelly would finally be able to build the roster the way he needed to contend. Once again, LSU lost a season opener to USC in Las Vegas. Breaking the fourth wall a bit: this was the game where I began to question if this Brian Kelly experiment would work out. The loss to Lincoln Riley and the Trojans was brutal, considering Riley was also a name on the hot board to replace Ed Orgeron when Kelly was hired. A six-game win streak followed the loss to Riley's USC before the Tigers would drop three straight to Texas A&M, Alabama and Florida, spanning from October 26 to November 16. The Tigers, led by Kelly, proved they were pretenders again, missing the playoff even in its first expanded year.

Maybe 2025 would be different after Kelly took the Tigers to Clemson and won their first season-opening game since 2019 in a hard-fought 17-10 battle. Kelly and LSU would rattle off three more wins before facing Kiffin and Ole Miss in Oxford in a top-15 matchup. This matchup with Ole Miss cemented two ideas in the minds of LSU fans. First, Garrett Nussmeier's injury situation was worse than advertised; second, if LSU decided to move on from Brian Kelly, Lane Kiffin would be a very entertaining coach to have in Baton Rouge.

LSU would drop that game and two more before the end of October, including the repugnant 49-25 loss to Texas A&M that saw the Tigers blow an 18-14 halftime lead, which resulted in the removal of Brian Kelly. Under interim head coach Frank Wilson, LSU would finish the regular season 2-2.

In 2022, Kiffin was the opponent Kelly defeated right before making the famous "contender" statement. In 2025, Kiffin was the coach whose top-15 matchup sealed the fate of Kelly's tenure in Baton Rouge. Now in 2026, Kiffin is the one standing at the podium in Baton Rouge, tasked with proving he is a contender. Yet 6-2 in 2026 carries a completely different weight than 6-2 did in 2022 or 2024.

2026 LSU at 6-2 is one of the most dangerous teams in the country. Most dangerous does not necessarily mean best; dangerous here means unpredictable, erratic, inscrutable, enigmatic. It is the tiger in an enclosure you know would maul you if ever given the chance. Brian Kelly's 6-2s felt more like Mike IV in 1981, escaping and wandering around campus, full of potential to cause damage but ultimately sedated with three tranquilizer darts and returned to his habitat.

The stats back the idea of LSU being more dangerous in 2026 than in years past. Through eight games, Kiffin's numbers are better than Kelly's four-season averages in every category (Kiffin first, Kelly second): yards per game, 510.0 to 440.4; yards allowed per game, 258.1 to 366.1; passing yards per game, 318.0 to 288.2; passing yards allowed per game, 172.8 to 222.7; rushing yards per game, 192.0 to 152.2; rushing yards allowed per game, 85.4 to 143.4; points per game, 40.1 to 33.3; and points allowed per game, 16.0 to 23.7. . It is, however, just eight games into the season; the numbers are hard to ignore, and with Alabama, Texas, Tennessee and Arkansas left on the horizon, those stats may be a bit inflated. A counterpoint to that is that Brian Kelly never had to play a nine-game conference schedule.

Kelly came the closest to a playoff berth in Year One. Can Kiffin and company do what Kelly never could and reach the playoffs this year and beyond? With the way Kiffin is building the roster and the program's philosophy, the same falloff would be unlikely. Only time will tell if this year's Tigers are contenders or pretenders.

#2836. INTERVIEW: Carsten Cramer relaxed about Dortmund's transfer practices despite failing to sign Köln's Said El Mala

MÜNCHEN (Bulinews): In Munich last weekend, Borussia Dortmund CEO Carsten Cramer stated the Westphalian club have not blown their cover after last summer’s prolonged transfer saga for 1.FC Köln star Said El Mala.

“From our perspective, we made a huge offer to them [Köln for El Mala] which maybe five years ago we wouldn’t have paid that much for a player,” Cramer explained at a round table event for which Bulinews.com was present.

“Numbers [in transfer fees] are changing at the moment, but we won’t pay ridiculous or stupid [prices] because we want to be a solid and serious club. No financial risks will be taken for successes.

The 20-year-old was heavily linked with BVB who, according to Sky Germany and BILD, offered fees of up to €50million but were rejected. In response to this, Cramer has no fears that the club’s historically cost-effective transfer methods have been exposed.

“We never mentioned the fee [for Said El Mala] publicly, so that [€50 million offer] is still a rumour. We just said we were interested to spend a huge amount of money,” he pointed out, casting doubt over their actual offer to the Cathedral City outfit.

“It can happen that [clubs will know Dortmund can now pay more for players] but that will not influence our way of negotiating. Everyone knows we are a powerful club, and we are a financially very healthy football club.

“We don’t need to hide our strengths. If we have an opportunity to spend money on a talented player which might sound a bit too expensive, if we are convinced, we might do it. I’m not concerned about [clubs knowing we can pay more],” he added.

Late last August, Köln would agree a contract extension with their talisman El Mala until June 2031. Could Dortmund plan another approach in the future? Cramer was quick to suppress the idea and avoid further rumours developing.

“We are happy with our squad; everyone is fully convinced with it. We decided to stop our negotiations with Köln because we had good ideas in mind and not only going down the El Mala route.

“It showed everyone that Dortmund is interested to make some special signings. What we have done with [Giannis] Konstantelias, [Kostas] Karetsas and [Joey] Veerman was really progressive from our perspective.

“We spent a huge amount of money for them, and don’t forget we have [Joane] Gadou who we hired very early from Salzburg. He may be cheap given his potential, but he cost money as well.

“No decision is done regarding how we proceed in the next transfer windows. We watch the market and there is no further comment regarding any player including El Mala, however his quality still exists,” Dortmund’s CEO concluded.

#2834. The Great Divide: Who is MMA’s worst referee?

When the dust settles on fight night, the last thing fans want to be talking about is the third man in the cage.

And yet, far too often these days we find ourselves coming out of an event with the biggest talking point being some form of officiating gaffe. Case in point, veteran referee Dan Miragliotta became MMA's main character this week after an inexplicable standup call that might have directly led to Tom Nolan defeating Renato Moicano in the UFC Vegas 123 main event.

Unfortunately for Miragliotta, this has led to plenty of discussion as to whether he is the worst active referee in all of MMA. And if not him, then who?

Keeping in mind that officiating is a mostly thankless job where only the top names in the biggest shows make substantial pay, MMA Fighting's Alexander K. Lee and Jed Meshew make their picks for the two referees who make fans and fighters the most nervous.

Lee: Sorry, but "The Gold Standard" has become "The Mold Standard."

To say Herb Dean has lost his fastball is really an insult to baseball pitchers who are still able to eat up innings with savvy and guile. Experience is no substitute for negligence, and Dean has exhibited much more of the latter than the former in recent years. I know fans still have a lot of affection for Dean as he was a familiar face during the UFC's boom period and is still hanging around in the TKO world domination era, but at this point even the staunchest Dean supporter has to be loosening their grip on the past.

Remember that amazing stoppage he made when Frank Mir broke Tim Sylvia's arm, saving Sylvia from further injury? That was great. It was also 22 years ago.

That's not to say Dean hasn't had his moments since, but what's made him absolutely brutal to watch now is his inconsistency.

Sometimes he stops fights out of nowhere.

He refuses to take points. He fakes out fighters, making them think he's about to stop a fight, then backs off (hence another nickname, "Hokey Pokey Herb"). And heaven help any fighter that has to deal with Dean in a video review. Dean is lucky The Ultimate Fighter viewership isn't what it used to be, because his egregious mishandling of the Xavier Franklin situation went mostly overlooked.

ICYMI: In the final minute of a tournament semifinal between Franklin and Ilimbek Akylbek Uulu, Dean stepped in to stop the action with Franklin delivering a finishing flurry and was clearly heard saying, "It's over. The fight's done." However, Akylbek Uulu complained he was poked in the eye, so Dean decided to go to video review and later claimed he called for a timeout, not a stoppage. Franklin went on to lose on the cards.

In an interview with MMA Fighting, Franklin called Dean "a lying bastard."

All of that is just the tip of the iceberg, as fighter after fighter has spoken out against Dean, who has been living off of his once-sterling reputation and past accomplishments. Imagine being an athlete stepping into the cage not knowing whether you can trust the referee to make the right decision with your career—and health—potentially in his hands. That's the roll of the dice every fighter takes when they see Herb Dean's name on the bout sheet.

Just for fun, here's some additional reading:

Meshew: If we had debated this just a week ago, I would firmly be on board with AK's breakdown. While Herb Dean may have once been the best referee in the sport (it's true!), those days are long, LONG past. Every point AK brings against Mr. Dean is true, and I won't pretend to argue against it. But I have a compelling counter-argument for who is truly the most hapless current referee:

I've been watching MMA for over 20 years, and that is the single worst piece of officiating I've ever seen. Even on a regional level, that would be egregious, much less in the biggest organization in the world. But you don't have to take my word for it: basically every MMA person agrees.

And it might be different if this was a one-time occurrence. Any person can have a bad day at the office or a temporary moment of insanity. Those happen. But Dan Miragliotta has been a bad referee for many years at this point, as the bevy of "highlights" that cropped up on social media following the Moicano incident can show better than I could ever argue.

The last one is the real kicker: 25 minutes of poor performance. Yikes.

It should be acknowledged that being an MMA referee sucks. These men spend enormous amounts of time traveling to referee shows, and they're making at most a couple grand per event. Don't get me wrong, there are harder jobs, but it's not like people are getting rich doing this, and I can't imagine it's the most fun to have people boo and hate you for simply trying to do your job the best you can.

But none of that excuses poor refereeing. Miragliotta is a professional, and professionals are expected to do their job, especially when failure to do so can negatively impact someone else. Maybe Tom Nolan beats Moicano anyway, but maybe he doesn't, and we'll never know because Miragliotta took that away from him, simultaneously taking the crown of "Worst Referee in MMA" away from Dean at the same time.

#2833. NFL ranking of top 50 trade prospects is full of potential Bengals targets

The Cincinnati Bengals are 5-2 as they prepare for their Week 9 game in Madrid, Spain, against the 3-5 Atlanta Falcons. They're riding a two-game win streak, though the wins were ugly at times, and are very much in the mix to make a run at the AFC North title to host a playoff game for the first time since 2023.

Things aren't all sunshine and rainbows, though. The Bengals are dealing with some injuries, and many analysts believe they're aggressively pursuing an acquisition to help the team make a run. Considering they already traded the No. 10 overall selection in this year's draft to the Giants for Dexter Lawrence, a rare mid-season trade from the Bengals would likely blow the collective minds of fans across the globe.

Here are some of the players the Bengals could benefit from, in order from top to bottom on the list:

Taylor is one of the best running backs in the league and has been for some time. Since he was drafted in 2020, Taylor has more scrimmage yards than all RBs except for Derrick Henry. He is the type of explosive player who could change an offense. After firing GM Chris Ballard, the Colts should be considering all options, including a full tear-down and rebuild. Taylor signed a two-year extension with the Colts in August. Indianapolis would take on $10 million in dead money in 2027 if it traded Taylor, so the contract is not preventive.

This would have made sense a couple of weeks ago, but there are issues in the secondary that can't be ignored. Still, the Bengals do need to figure out how to fix their running game, because they'll need it in December and January.

Downs is in the final year of his rookie deal, and he has developed into one of the better route runners in the league. He is predominantly a slot player, aligning inside on more than 74 percent of his career offensive snaps. The Colts signed receiver Alec Pierce to a four-year, $114 million extension in the offseason. Pierce has played 49 snaps this season while battling injuries. Downs is good, cheap and on an expiring deal. He would be a potentially valuable trade piece if interim GM Ed Dodds is tasked with bolstering the draft cupboard.

Do the Bengals really need a wide receiver? No. But Downs could fit in nicely. He's a true slot receiver, and he would immediately be the Bengals' WR3, which is a spot currently held by TE1 Mike Gesicki. With some injuries at wide receiver, including to Andrei Iosivas, and the relative inexperience of everyone else, adding another talented receiver wouldn't hurt.

Though Hooker is under contract through 2028, he does not have any fully guaranteed money on his deal after this season. He is a versatile safety who can fulfill multiple responsibilities — post safety, split-field safety, nickel, dime, underneath zone and man-to-man on tight ends and slot receivers. He is a strong tackler who can impact in the running game, and he has the instincts in zone coverage to feel routes and bait quarterbacks into throws. The Titans would take on $8.6 million in dead money in 2027 if they traded Hooker.

How crazy would it be for Hooking to pick Joe Burrow off three times in Week 8 just to join him a couple of weeks later? The Bengals have dealt with injuries at safety. Bryan Cook has missed a couple of games, as has Kyle Dugger, and Jordan Battle has been hit or miss (mostly miss). A trade for Hooker could shore up the secondary.

Robertson signed a two-year, $16 million deal with the Commanders in free agency. He has been one of the few bright spots from Peters' offseason. Robertson does not have any fully guaranteed money on his deal in 2027. The Commanders would take on $3 million in dead money in 2027 if they trade him before the deadline. Robertson is a capable man coverage corner who could help a number of teams in the secondary. He can play inside and outside.

Here's really where the Bengals need some help, especially if DJ Turner is forced to miss some time. The cornerback position was pretty much an afterthought this offseason, and now they're potentially going to pay the piper for it. If the Bengals do make a move, I predict it will be for a corner.

Woolen won a Super Bowl with the Seahawks last season. He then hit free agency and, rather surprisingly, a market did not materialize for him. Woolen ended up signing a one-year deal with the Eagles. Although he has given up two touchdowns, Woolen has played well in coverage down-to-down for Philadelphia. He was in tight coverage on the Parker Washington one-handed touchdown in the Eagles' loss to the Jaguars in Week 5. The combination of size and speed will always make Woolen an intriguing piece.

Another possibility at corner. He could join Boye Mafe, whom he won a Super Bowl with in Seattle. He could fill in for a starter on the outside should the need arise. That way the Bengals wouldn't be forced to rely on Josh Newton, who reportedly spent much of the offseason in the doghouse.

Jackson is in the final year of a two-year free-agent deal he signed in 2025. He has missed the past two games with a hamstring injury. Jackson is one of the most compelling defensive backs on this list. He is on an expiring deal. He is relatively cheap, so he is an option for teams tight against the cap. And he is an experienced veteran who can acclimate quickly to a variety of schemes, though a zone-heavy scheme would be the best fit. Jackson has 23 career interceptions, tied for fifth-most among active players.

Same thing here. The Bengals could definitely use some help in the cornerback room. Even if Turner's heel injury allows him to play this weekend, will it limit him? He's required to be able to stay hip to hip with some of the best athletes in the world. If his foot hurts, will he be able to?

The Jets signed Wright to a one-year deal in free agency, and he has yet to play a defensive snap this season for coach Aaron Glenn. Wright should be a trade candidate even if the Jets win games over the next three weeks. He had five picks playing for the Chicago Bears in 2025. Wright lacks some burst and change-of-direction ability. But his ball production last season was very impressive. At 6-foot-4, he has receiver-like skills in 50-50 situations.

The Bengals were actually listed as one of the best fits for Wright, who had a good 2025 season but is struggling to get on the field this year. He could be had for little and potentially make a major impact for Al Golden's secondary.

Pollard, who signed with the Titans in free agency in 2024, is on an expiring contract. He has been getting the bulk of the work in the Tennessee backfield over Spears. Pollard is a veteran doubles hitter with some vision. He is reliable in pass protection. Pollard has the potential to be a supplemental piece in a running back rotation.

Pollard carried the ball 21 times for 117 yards and two touchdowns against the Bengals in Week 8. He might not be as flashy as Taylor or Saquon Barkley, but he would probably help. At least more than Tahj Brooks.

There were obviously others, but these were just some that caught my eye.

What trade targets from the list (and not on the list) are you most interested in for the Bengals before the Nov. 10 deadline?

The halfway point of the 2026 NFL season arrives this weekend. Next week, Dianna Russini apparently will return to sports media.

The Athletic conducted a review of her work. Its findings were released in early September.

“Russini’s relationship with Vrabel was in clear violation of The Athletic’s standards,” wrote Mike Semel of The Athletic, who conducted the investigation. “Regardless of whether the relationship was romantic, it was a breach and should have been disclosed.”

Beyond the relationship was the manner in which she handled the emergence of the controversy.

"[W]hen first confronted with the photos by The New York Post,” Semel wrote, “Russini waited two days before telling her editors and managers. She then told a story to explain the photos that did not align with facts, raising issues of trust.”

Along the way, a strange story emerged regarding Russini being pulled over for texting while driving — made stranger by her decision to tell the story publicly and embellish the notion that she FaceTimed a head coach for help in getting out of the ticket.

So if she’ll be reporting again, she’ll need to restore her own credibility. Especially given the unique set of facts that resulted in her departure from The Athletic.

"We Are Youth | Talent of the Month" is Juventus.com's monthly feature that introduces you to the stars of Next Gen and the Bianconeri's youth teams.

The star of October 2026 is Next Gen striker Arman Durmisi, who is 18 years old. Her spoke to us about his early days in Slovenia alongside his brother Dajan, through his debut in Serie C, to the thrilling experiences he's had with the First Team.

"I started playing football when I was very young. I played lots of sports, I also played volleyball, handball and basketball, but in the end, football was the one I liked best of all. I can't quite remember the very first time I touched a ball, but my first clear memory is of a match when I was very young: it was raining and I scored my first goal. I was absolutely delighted after that day, it's a really lovely memory. As a child, I played in just about every position, but when I scored that first goal, I realised straight away that that was where I belonged."

There is one fundamental constant in Arman's journey: his family and the figure of his father, a pillar of support for both him and his brother as they grew up.

"My family has been absolutely vital. My father has always supported both me and my brother. To me, he is a role model I will never forget, because he gave his all to ensure we could reach certain heights. Without him, I'd never have made it to a place like this. My brother and I have travelled most of this journey together, it's been brilliant playing with him because he knows me so well. I hope that one day we'll be able to play together again, or perhaps face each other as opponents in a big match."

"Joining a big club like Juventus alongside my brother made it even better. Everything was new here, new people, a new environment, but as there were two of us, we helped each other out. At first we didn't speak the language and it was a bit difficult, but in my first year, two of my compatriots, Raffaele Huli and Kris Gecaj, helped me a great deal. And off the pitch? I'm happy in Turin; it's a lovely city and at Juve you really have everything you need, nothing's missing. In my spare time, I like playing on the PlayStation with my friends and chatting on the phone with my closest friends who've stayed behind in Slovenia. Whenever I've got a few days off, I go back to see them."

"I'm a player who lives to score goals; if I had to describe myself to someone who doesn't know me, that's how I'd put it. My childhood idol has always been Lionel Messi, even though I don't play in his position. But amongst the strikers who have always inspired me and whom I like the most is Luis Suárez. He's always been ruthless in front of goal, technically brilliant, knows how to play as part of the team and can do practically everything. And then another source of inspiration is definitely Zlatan Ibrahimović."

"In Slovenia, after playing in the youth ranks, I took the next step up to the first team and really felt the difference. In these environments, you grow not only physically but, above all, mentally. The most important thing is your mindset; if you have confidence in yourself, you play more calmly and then things just fall into place on the pitch. The move from the Under-20s to Next Gen amongst the professionals is helping me a great deal. Serie C is an extremely tough league. The defenders are bigger and more experienced, and there's a lot of tactical play.

"With Coach Brambilla's staff, we're focusing particularly on our defensive play. Sometimes a striker just wants to attack, but in today's football, you also need to help the team. It's a learning curve to eventually make it into the first team. At the moment, I'm getting on really well with my teammates. I get on well with everyone, including the manager. I talk a lot with his coaching staff, who give me daily advice on how to keep raising my game. Playing for Juve isn't like playing for just any club – it has a massive history. Knowing that the club has faith in me makes me absolutely delighted and really motivates me. I'm on the right track so far, but it's always up to me to keep performing well."

The summer gave Arman a taste of the very highest level as he trained with the first team and took part in the international tour: "Training with the first team was a wonderful experience. The standard is very high and the ball moves faster, but when you play with such strong teammates, they ultimately help you play well too. At first you feel a bit out of your depth, but then you get used to it because the players talk to you and put you at ease. The tour of China and Australia was brilliant; I even played in a match. Sharing the pitch and the attack with players of the calibre of Kenan Yildiz and Edon Zhegrova, or opponents like Estevao, is incredible. Sometimes you wonder if it's real because everything's moving so fast. At first I was a bit nervous, but it was the right kind of nervousness, without any anxiety. Then, as soon as you step onto the pitch, you forget everything and just focus on playing."

"I haven't done too much planning for this season, but the main aim is to do well with the Next Gen side, developing both as a team and as a player. It would also be fantastic to make my debut and score a goal for the First Team. My biggest dream is to win something important in this shirt. And my dream from when I was a child? Well, I think it's the same as everyone else's: to win the Ballon d'Or."

#2814. Why it is a blessing in disguise that Novak Djokovic has failed to qualify for the ATP Finals this year

Novak Djokovic's desperate late bid to qualify for the ATP Finals has sadly come to an end, thwarted at the hands of Rinky Hijikata.

Just as the draw appeared to have opened up for the Serbian at the Paris Masters, with Alex de Minaur, Frances Tiafoe and Alexander Zverev all losing, he was next to suffer a shock defeat in just the second round.

Having battled so bravely to defeat Valentin Vacherot in the very first round, many expected his next match to be simple by comparison.

Djokovic insisted he should have won the match, but conceded that his opponent played well despite gifting him the victory.

Now, his season is over, and it is time for him to rest and recover ahead of the 2027 campaign.

Whilst his inability to qualify for the ATP Finals will likely sting now, in all honesty, this could end up being a huge blessing in disguise for the 39-year-old.

Novak Djokovic's chances to win a 25th Grand Slam title are decreasing with each passing year. That much is clear.

However, twice in 2026 he proved he is still more than capable of stringing incredible runs together, and actually started the season off by reaching the Australian Open final, beating Jannik Sinner and snatching the first set off Carlos Alcaraz before eventually losing.

Then, later on in the year at Wimbledon, he reached the semi-finals again, but was well beaten by the Italian superstar.

It feels like for years now, injuries and fitness concerns have plagued this great champion at crucial moments.

Djokovic has even revealed he has been dealing with a health issue which has held him back massively, though he recently admitted he felt like a solution was close.

So, perhaps some extra time off to return fully recovered in Melbourne might be perfect, especially considering he has already proved it is likely his best bet at finally winning a record-breaking 25th major title.

The chances of him accomplishing this feat now seem hugely slim, and Djokovic will be aware of that.

However, if he is to give himself the best possible chance of achieving the unthinkable, playing the ATP Finals and extending his season by another two and a half weeks from today likely wouldn't have been the best course of action.

#2813. Eagles-Commanders somehow breaks 19 million viewers

When George Costanza pitched the show about nothing to NBC president Russell Dalrymple, Dalrymple asked, “Well, why am I watching it?”

More than 30 years later, that sentiment still applies. As evidenced by the fact that, per Nielsen, 19.015 million (on average) watched Sunday night’s snoozefest between the Eagles and Commanders on the network that Dalrymple once ran.

It’s an amazing number, given that it was the 2-5 Eagles against the 1-4-1 Commanders. The game itself wasn’t particularly compelling, and it followed afternoon windows that culminated in a down-to-the-wire showdown between the Chiefs and the Broncos.

The league could have flexed the game out of the evening window. It chose not to. In the end, the not-ready-for-prime-time game managed to attract far more viewers than anyone would have expected.

It helped that there wasn’t a 9:30 a.m. ET game in Week 8. Fourteen straight hours of football is a lot, even for the most ardent fan.

Then again, Commanders-Eagles was a lot. Even for the most ardent fan. And more than 19 million nevertheless watched the game.

That's the right mentality to have. If the Jets are going to upset the Chiefs, who are a 10-point favorite at home, they have to believe in themselves. The green and white have the pieces in place to pull off the upset. They have offensive pieces to be able to score points, but with how the Jets' defense has performed, they might need to win this track meet 55-50.

#2805. Jack Campbell: I have full movement in my lower body, and am making progress with movement in my upper body

Lions linebacker Jack Campbell has issued a statement on Wednesday after suffering a serious neck injury on Sunday, saying that he has full movement in his lower body and is continuing to make progress with movement in his upper body.

This is the first definitive update on Campbell’s condition since he was transported to the hospital on Sunday.

“I’m incredibly encouraged by the progress I’ve made in such a short period of time,” Campbell’s statement reads, in part. “I have full movement in my lower body, and I’m continuing to make progress with movement in my upper body. I know there’s still work ahead, but I remain very optimistic. I’m taking things one day at a time, staying positive, and focusing on getting better.”

Campbell went on to thank those who have helped take care of him since Sunday.

“I especially want to thank the athletic trainers and medical personnel who responded and cared for me on the field,” Campbell said. “I know those were difficult moments, and I’m incredibly grateful for the professionalism, compassion, and care you showed me. The way you handled everything and looked after me when I needed it most is something I’ll never forget. From the bottom of my heart, thank you.

“I also can’t say enough about the incredible care I’ve received from the medical team at Henry Ford Hospital and the Detroit Lions medical staff. They’ve been amazing to me and my family throughout this process, and I’m truly grateful for everything they’ve done.”

Campbell added, “To my teammates, coaches, and everyone in the Lions organization, I want you to know how much I love and appreciate you. This team is a family to me, and the way everyone has been there for me means everything. I’m proud to be a Detroit Lion and couldn’t ask to be surrounded by a better group of people.

“One thing I’ve learned about Detroit is that this city is built on toughness, resilience, and grit. That’s exactly how I’m going to approach this challenge.

“Please continue to keep me and my family in your prayers. We feel the love, and I can’t thank everyone enough.”

#2804. Victor Wembanyama makes NBA history with 52-point, 24-rebound, 8-block game in Spurs win

Victor Wembanyama has had a heck of a career as he plays his fourth NBA season. But nothing matches what he did on Wednesday.

The San Antonio Spurs superstar set a new career high in scoring with 52 points plus 24 rebounds and 8 blocks in a 112-111 win over the Dallas Mavericks. No player in NBA history has posted those totals since blocks became an official stat in 1973, and only one other player had posted even a 50-20-5 game (Bob McAdoo, Feb 22, 1974).

To put Wembanyama's game in additional historical context:

He was the first player in NBA history to have at least 25 points, 15 rebounds and five blocks in a half.

He was the first player who had at least 50 points and 20 rebounds in a one-point victory since Wilt Chamberlain in 1964, according to ESPN

His 15-for-15 performance at the foul line in the first half tied James Harden for the most free throws without a miss in the first half during the play-by-play era since 1997-98

His eight blocks were the most for a player who had a 50-point game since blocks became official in 1973-75

He became the fifth player ever with more than one 50-point game at age 22 or younger

The game came down to the final possessions, with Wembanyama making a free throw to give the Spurs the lead and Kyrie Irving missing a would-be game-winner right before the buzzer.

It was a tough shot for Irving, who had P.J. Washington unguarded on the perimeter but opted for a contested turnaround jump shot that missed the rim.

Wembanyama was clearly on pace for history from early in the game, eventually entering the locker room after becoming the first player to post at least 25 points, 15 rebounds and 5 blocks in a single half. It was a dominant half for both him and the Spurs, who led by 17 at halftime and as much as 19 in the third quarter.

The Mavericks, however, came back with Cooper Flagg and Naji Marshall leading the charge and at one point led by three in the fourth quarter. The Spurs were in dire straits around then, as Wembanyama briefly exited the game with an apparent ankle injury.

Wembanyama returned and helped the Spurs hold on. San Antonio outscored Dallas by 23 points during his 34 minutes, and got outscored by 22 in the 14 minutes back-up center Luke Kornet was playing.

"I can still do more," Wembanyama said, per the San Antonio Express-News. "My shots weren't falling tonight, and that forces me into a style of play that is exhausting. I can do it. I mean the proof is here I can do it, but I can be much better if my shots fell."

Not only was Wembanyama temporarily hobbled, he also revealed after the game that he's been dealing with an illness. He said he was still sick Wednesday, but no longer felt as weak as he did while dealing with a virus:

"I haven't been feeling great lately. I've been sick. Today felt like I was getting my legs back. It should be more like this more often."

Wembanyama posted 12 points on 5-of-15 shooting with 11 rebounds, 5 assists and 3 blocks in his previous game, a win over the Utah Jazz. In the game directly before that, he dropped 43 in another win over the Minnesota Timberwolves. That was the second-highest scoring game of his career, and is now the third-highest.

The win improves the Spurs' record to 6-2, tied for fourth-best in a competitive Western Conference. The Mavericks are now tied for 10th at 4-4.

#2803. Landing at an Airport Near You: The New Florida Panthers jetBlue Plane

DANIA BEACH — Ever wanted to fly on the Florida Panthers plane? Now, thanks to jetBlue, you can.

On Thursday morning, the newest entry into the jetBlue specially themed aircraft collection was unveiled at Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International airport.

Sasha Barkov, Brad Marchand, and Bill Zito were among those in attendance for the official unveiling.

The Airbus A320 is painted in Panthers red with the 'creeping' panther (from the team's secondary shoulder logo) adorning the side with the team's shield logo on the tail.

The team's stick-and-palm logo also makes an appearance on the plane's livery — one which has the special designation 'Go Cats Go.'

JetBlue has been a longtime sponsor of the team and FLL is one of the airline's main hubs so, a special Panthers-themed plane is a natural fit.

After all, the airline already has done up some of their jets with the colors and logos of the Boston Bruins, Celtics, and Red Sox as well as the Brooklyn Nets.

They even have a Dunkin' themed plane as well as planes honoring the FDNY, I ❤️ NY, and the New York Jets.

The airline has its corporate headquarters in Long Island City, NY.

Although the plane's new look is officially being unveiled this morning, it has already been in use, flying from JFK to the Dominican Republic before landing in Fort Lauderdale on Wednesday for the ceremony in Dania Beach.

Air Cat One is scheduled to fly from FLL to Boston Logan later this afternoon.

#2802. Josh Jacobs: "There's a lot of stuff being said about me that's completely false"

On Friday, Wisconsin authorities released documents in the Josh Jacobs criminal case that included three allegations against him from other women. On Wednesday, Jacobs spoke directly to reporters for the first time since the material became public.

“It’s one of those things for me where it’s like, it really feels like an attack on me and who I am and my character,” Jacobs said, via Rob Demovsky of ESPN. “And at the end of the day, there’s a lot of stuff being said about me that’s completely false -- like, completely made up, and it’s like people just run with it. And I can’t change that.

“It’s just one of those things where it’s like, OK, all I can do is try to be who I am and try not to let the negative moments change who I am. And that was the biggest thing for me throughout this whole process. I didn’t want to go to a place where I felt like I was closed off and I’m angry all the time because of what’s going on in my life.”

The situation would be very different if Jacobs hadn’t pleaded no contest to a misdemeanor battery charge arising from an incident in May 2026. Admitting to an incident of violence against a woman makes it harder for him to credibly claim that three other women who contacted authorities about Jacobs doing the same thing are making it all up.

Still, Jacobs believes the newly-surfaced allegations won’t result in more missed time, following the six-game stint on paid leave arising from the most recent incident.

“With all the evidence that we have and that they have at this point, it’s not one of those things where I’m sitting back on my hands like, ‘OK, am I going to play this week?’” Jacobs said. “It’s like, I kind of already know what it is, so it’s like . . . it’s really just up to them to make their final decision. But like I’m not worried about feeling like I’m going to miss any more time than I already have.”

The league continues to investigate Jacobs, and it’s investigating the recent allegations, too. Through it all, the Packers have been linked on multiple occasions to a potential trade for Colts running back Jonathan Taylor. If the Packers land Taylor, it could mean that they’ll move on from Jacobs.

#2801. The 'Peanut Punch' is part of NFL's forced-fumble surge. What is it?

Pittsburgh Steelers defensive back Jamel Dean had his eyes in the backfield when New Orleans Saints quarterback Tyler Shough took the shotgun snap, faked the handoff and darted for the right pylon.

The Steelers were protecting a seven-point lead in a game they eventually won 16-10. Dean matched Shough's effort to turn the corner and reach the end zone by running parallel to the goal line. Then he made the calculated decision that Shough would dive for the pylon. Once the second-year signal-caller "declared," as Dean put it, Dean punched where he guessed the ball would be in that critical moment of intersection and collision.

What happened next has played out across the NFL all season long. The ball came loose, hit the pylon (to be ruled a touchback) and Dean turned a potential game-tying play into a game-saving one because of the prevalence of the "Peanut Punch," named after former Chicago Bears cornerback Charles "Peanut" Tillman who perfected the move and harassed ballcarriers for more than a decade.

"Now it's almost like they're expecting me to get the ball out, now that I've shown that I'm capable of doing it," Dean told USA TODAY Sports.

Las Vegas Raiders linebacker Nakobe Dean, who is tied for second in the league with 3 forced fumbles, said hunting the ball is drilled into every defender.

"But I guess I can say I've put a bit of an extra emphasis on it than I ever have this year," he told USA TODAY Sports.

Through eight weeks of play, forced fumbles have increased by 32.3 percent year-over-year – 2025 was an especially down year for forced fumbles. In 2026, there have been average of 1.73 forced fumbles per game. The Raiders lead all teams with 12 forced fumbles, while the New York Jets, Steelers and Cleveland Browns all enter Week 9 with 10.

Nakobe Dean doesn't necessarily classify his successful forced fumbles as punches. They are more of a slap, he said. But the tactic speaks to the league-wide uptick, Nakobe Dean said, because defenders are not sacrificing a tackle during the strip attempt.

"You see guys who have mastered getting a punch on a ball and also making a tackle, which is harder than what you would imagine if you're making a real attempt at the ball," he said.

The "Peanut Punch" is coached league-wide, and every second defender into a scrum as the tackle is being made by a teammate is always searching for the ball. Some of Nakobe Dean's college coaches at Georgia spoke about the importance, but his pro coaches have always put a greater emphasis on trying to knock the ball loose from ballcarriers.

That trend is now flowing up from the college level, Nakobe Dean said, with rookies such as Jacob Rodriguez of the Miami Dolphins having already perfected the maneuver, according to ESPN analyst Louis Riddick. Rodriguez had seven forced fumbles during his final season at Texas Tech.

"He's a turnover machine," Riddick said during draft coverage in April.

Rodriguez's first successful NFL "Peanut Punch" came during a Week 8 loss, when the linebacker flew in and punched the ball out of the cradle of New England Patriots wide receiver Efton Chism.

"You see his attempts on the ball," Nakobe Dean noted before Rodriguez popped one out.

Running the ball and controlling the clock is in vogue again. Teams are relying on multiple tight-end formations in that effort. Risk aversion in the passing game is another factor.

The new kickoff rule and the constraints placed on defenders from an officiating standpoint makes for a "very offensive game," Baltimore Ravens defensive back Kyle Hamilton said. The defense needs every opportunity to give the ball back to the offense.

"That's something that's preached around the league on a daily basis," Hamilton told USA TODAY Sports. "It's funny seeing younger guys coming into the league during camp, especially ballcarriers, realize how many guys are going to be punching at the ball at this level. There's kind of a growing period with that, with some offensive guys. It's definitely more of an emphasis at this level, I would say, than college."

Jamel Dean wasn't punching at the rate he is now at the start of his career. But he said there is a higher premium on forced fumbles in 2026.

"Interceptions don't come that often, but at least you can make an effort play on a tackle – shoot, you got more attempts at that," said Dean, who also has three forced fumbles on the season.

And turnovers are "oxygen" for NFL defenses, as Browns defensive coordinator Mike Rutenberg said while discussing one of his unit's 10 forced fumbles – this one specifically coming via a punchout – this season.

"The ball's our oxygen," he told reporters. "I'm sure I get boring saying it, but it's in our DNA. It's what we believe in. We have opportunities in practice and periods to practice it. It's what (head coach Todd Monken) believes in. It's one of the keys to winning football games, is taking the ball away."

Like Rodriguez, other players around the league have garnered a reputation for being punchers. Los Angeles Rams linebacker Nate Landman forced two fumbles by Buffalo Bills linebacker James Cook that nearly swung the outcome of an overtime "Monday Night Football" game. Atlanta Falcons safety Jessie Bates is one of the league's best at the "Peanut Punch," evidenced by his forced fumble to save a touchdown in his team's Week 8 loss to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. But Fred Warner of the San Francisco 49ers may have the current top billing, with he and the Browns' Quincy Williams tied for the league lead in forced fumbles (4).

The "Peanut Punch" isn't going anywhere from a rule or enforcement standpoint.

"Ball security means everything in this game," NFL vice president of operations Troy Vincent said at the fall league meeting last month – sounding every bit like the former pro cornerback he is. "The onus is on the player to protect that ball."

Defensive players run the risk of drawing a penalty with a hit to the helmet or facemask. But the bigger danger is to themselves and their own hands. During training camp, Nakobe Dean said, his hand became caught in a facemask after he tried a punch. Shoulder pads, helmets, forearms, elbows – none feel good despite being the aggressor, Dean said.

"It's the price of admission … my hands sometimes be sore," he said.

Jamel Dean came across Tillman highlights about a year ago – a game in which he forced three fumbles was in his social-media algorithm – and he said to himself, "dude, he's a ballhawk, I got to start chances like him."

Tillman finished sixth all time on the NFL forced fumbles list (44, including 10 during his 2012 All-Pro season). He was not available through the Bears, although his post-playing career has been interesting itself – he became a FBI agent but left the agency in 2025 and now works for the NBA in a gambling integrity role.

Forcing fumbles is part of the Steelers' culture, Jamel Dean said. That's one way to fit in during his first year with his new organization.

Defenders are constantly looking for opportunities when the ballcarrier finds himself in a vulnerable position. The signals, Jamel Dean said, can occur when a runner is making a cut "and they get kind of real wide when they cut with their arms." A player exposing the ball while reaching or diving is another prime window for a punch. But striking while the ballcarrier is going to the ground is key, he said.

"The more attempts you get," Dean said, "the higher the chance of it actually coming out."

#2799. Luka Dončić has fan sitting courtside removed after incident with official during Lakers' win over Kings

Los Angeles Lakers star Luka Dončić had a fan sitting courtside at the Golden 1 Center removed on Wednesday night after an incident between the fan and one of the game's officials.

As he was set to inbound the ball late in the third quarter of the Lakers' 116-103 win over the Sacramento Kings, Dončić suddenly started calling officials and security over on the baseline while pointing to a man sitting in a courtside seat. The man had caught the ball on the previous play and launched it back aggressively at the official, who was not prepared for it. The ball hit her awkwardly, which Dončić clearly didn't like.

"What the f*** are you doing?" Dončić appeared to ask the fan before calling over others.

"He just tossed it really strong, the ball, toward the ref," Dončić said after the game, per ESPN. "I just asked him what the hell he's doing."

Officials stopped the game briefly and quickly approached the man. He was then walked out.

The game then continued on without incident. It's unclear if the man said anything back to Dončić.

The Lakers took a seven-point lead into the locker room at halftime, and then surged ahead in the second half to secure the 13-point win on Wednesday night. Dončić continued his offensive tear, and finished with 40 points, 9 rebounds and 7 assists. He shot 11 of 23 from the field. Dončić has scored at least 40 points in five of his last six outings, which includes a 52-point night late last month.

Austin Reaves added 21 points for the Lakers in the win. Walker Kessler finished with 15 points and eight rebounds. The Lakers now sit at 7-2 on the season.

Darius Acuff led the Kings with 22 points and 12 assists in the loss, which dropped them to 1-7 and 0-3 on their home court. Zach LaVine finished with 21 points, and Domantas Sabonis had 16 points and 17 rebounds.

Dončić and the Lakers will be back in action on Friday against the Portland Trail Blazers.

#2798. Nick Bosa returns to practice with limited work

49ers defensive end Nick Bosa returned to practice Wednesday after missing the team’s past five games with a calf injury. Bosa was a limited participant.

“It’s a long year, and I kind of just reminded myself that I need to be ready for the long haul,” Bosa said, via Harrison Rich of the San Francisco Chronicle.

Bosa tore his right ACL in a Sept. 21, 2025, game against the Cardinals and underwent surgery five days later. As he was coming back this summer, Bosa experienced soreness and tendinitis in his right knee, and the 49ers backed him down until Sept. 2 when he returned to practice.

He injured his left calf while warming up in practice for Week 3.

“I must have had some type of compensation going on, especially in that first week back,” Bosa said. “I was kind of trying to push it back with the [right knee] tendinitis, so I may have been favoring [the left calf] a little bit. I was just doing my normal warm-up drills one day, and I tweaked it. Calves are a pretty long process. I’ve never had one, so it took a little longer than I expected, but I don’t even think about it anymore.”

Wide receiver Mike Evans (ribs/Achilles) remained out of practice, and running back Christian McCaffrey (hamstring) also didn’t practice.

Victor Wembanyama scored a career-high 52 points, and the San Antonio Spurs needed every single one of them in a close game against the rival Dallas Mavericks. Despite blowing a 19-point lead, the Spurs were able to hold on in the fourth quarter to win 112-11.

Wembanyama dominated the game in every aspect. He added 24 points and 8 blocks to his 52 points. In the end, it was his final free throw (after missing four straight previous free throws) that won San Antonio the game.

Shortly after that free throw, Kyrie Irving had a chance to win the game, but missed a mid-range jump shot while guarded heavily by De'Aaron Fox. Irving led the charge for the Mavericks, scoring 29 points on 9-for-27 shooting from the field. Dallas got a spark off the bench from Naji Marshall, who went off in the second half for 22 points.

The win extends the Spurs' winning streak to 6 games. Next, they'll head to Sacramento for a rematch with the Kings on Friday.

The Spurs dominated the paint, outscoring the Mavs 62-40 in the paint and outrebounding Dallas 61-50. Both teams were hammering the offensive glass, as San Antonio grabbed 22 offensive boards, and Dallas had 18 offensive rebounds.

San Antonio needed to dominate the paint because they had one of the worst shooting nights they've had in a while. The Spurs shot just 39% from the field and went 5-for-36 from three, hitting just 14% of their deep shots.

There was a night-and-day difference when Wembanyama was on the court and when he was off it. He was +23 in the win, and Luke Kornet, the backup center, was -22 in his 14 minutes. That may be more indicative of how good Wembanyama was, but the team struggled mightily with the bench unit in the game.

Fox should get a lot of credit for his defense in that final possession against Irving. He kept pace with one of the shiftiest guards in the league and got a great contest on his mid-range jump shot.

It wasn't Stephon Castle's best shooting night, as he had 17 points on 6-of-20 shooting from the field. However, he responded late in the game, scoring back-to-back baskets when the Spurs needed them.

Dylan Harper's athleticism was on full display on his way to 21 points. He had some incredible finishes over and around the Mavericks' defenders, including a huge alley-oop dunk in the first half.

San Antonio's offense has looked its best when it's forcing switches in the pick-and-roll. When small guards get onto Wembanyama, the Spurs' guards have gotten so good at finding him for lobs or easy post-up buckets. That was on full display against the Mavs.

#2793. INTERVIEW: Patrick Owomoyela "wasn't aiming for BVB" move until a close friend convinced him

MÜNCHEN (Bulinews) Speaking at a media event attended by Bulinews.com, Patrick Owomoyela revealed a close friend was the real reason behind his 2008 move from Werder Bremen to Borussia Dortmund.

“When I was at Werder Bremen, they were like the challenger to Bayern Munich. I was there for three years, we always came third or second, but we were right there," Owomoyela explained.

“In my time, when I signed the contract [for Dortmund] that was it, I didn’t look anywhere else. I know this is very different today, their agents have plans. Now when players sign a contract they already know where they want to go next.

"I was already enjoying my time at the club I was with [Werder Bremen]. Borussia Dortmund wasn’t looking all too fancy and sexy back then. They almost came out of bankruptcy and had lots of different coaches. I wasn’t aiming for BVB.

“When that [Dortmund’s offer], came up, I had a friend in the stadium who was playing at Dortmund. So I knew about the stadium, the energy and how cool that could be [to play in front of]. He told me about the culture and fans.

“It was Otto Addo, I grew up with him in Hamburg. Like me he was a guy from Hamburg that had an African background that made it pro. I would visit him sometimes [in Dortmund].

“He had worked with Jurgen Klopp before so he got me thinking they could be building something big. I wasn’t [planning on] going [to Dortmund] to be Bundesliga champion, that was way out of the picture at the time,” Owomoyela chuckled.

Little did he know, less than four seasons later he and Klopp would be celebrating winning back-to-back German topflight titles, as well as a 5-2 DFB-Pokal triumph over FC Bayern Munich.

#2791. Amazon’s ‘Terrell & T.O.’ examines Terrell Owens: a man and a showman

The Prime Video documentary Terrell & T.O. is unlikely to change anyone's opinions on Terrell Owens.

If you're entrenched in your belief that Terrell Owens is a narcissistic ego monster who wrecked team chemistry, that will remain your viewpoint. If you're adamant that he is a misunderstood Hall of Famer who loves to have fun, that will remain your assessment.

After watching this documentary, the fairest and most accurate depiction may lie in the middle. Terrell & T.O., which is available to stream on Nov. 5, revisits one of the most polarizing figures in NFL history. Owens didn't merely see himself as a football player, but as an entertainer as well. He coined the phrase "Get your popcorn ready" because he was a showman. He was the epitome of the diva wide receiver: highly productive and high maintenance.

As difficult as Owens could be, his greatness is undeniable. When his career ended after the 2010 season, Owens ranked second all time in receiving yards (15,934), behind only his former San Francisco 49ers teammate Jerry Rice (22,895). He was surpassed for second place by Larry Fitzgerald (17,492). Owens is also third in receiving touchdowns (153), trailing Rice (197) and Randy Moss (156).

And yet, the controversies surrounding Owens are what most people think of first. This is even though he never got into any criminal trouble and was readily accessible to the media. To be fair, Owens brought a lot of negative publicity on himself with some of the things he said and did. But the media also treated him unfairly at times, particularly Skip Bayless. Owens waited three years before NFL voters finally selected him for the Hall of Fame Class of 2018. That's a joke.

In Terrell & T.O., Owens goes into more detail about why he decided not to attend the Hall of Fame ceremony in Canton. Instead, he made his acceptance speech at his alma mater, UT Chattanooga. Owens was a third-round pick from a small school who reached the heights of his profession. The T.O. we know today is not who Terrell Owens was growing up.

Director Alexandria Stapleton shows viewers a different side of the Owens story that some may not know. Growing up in tiny Alexander City, Tennessee, he was raised by his grandmother and mother. There were family secrets Owens originally wasn't aware of. Those likely impacted his development. In his formative years, Owens was described as introverted. A sharp contrast to what he would eventually become.

An armchair psychologist could see how his upbringing contributed to his personality explosion as he rose to fame. Owens grew to love the attention that scoring touchdowns brought.

But his insatiable hunger for the limelight also caused problems for him, his teammates, and coaches. His turbulent 2-year stint with the Philadelphia Eagles defined his career. He was lauded for playing in the Super Bowl with a broken leg. He also clashed with Donovan McNabb and Andy Reid. He was suspended for insubordination in 2005 while seeking a contract extension. The video of Owens doing shirtless sit-ups in his driveway in front of the media will live on forever in Philly sports lore.

Owens played for the 49ers, Eagles, Dallas Cowboys, Buffalo Bills, and Cincinnati Bengals. He excelled on the field throughout his career. But his greatness was always overshadowed by his antics and his reputation. In Terrell & T.O., it says a lot that two of his former quarterbacks, Steve Young and Tony Romo, speak highly of him.

"From my perspective, he was a great teammate," Romo said.

Terrell & T.O. will be available to stream starting on Nov. 5 on Amazon Prime Video.

#2790. Josh Allen and James Cook can both top 5,000 career rushing yards on Monday night

Bills quarterback Josh Allen and running back James Cook can both reach a big career milestone on Monday night against the Vikings.

Allen and Cook may both reach 5,000 career rushing yards: Allen currently has 4,991 rushing yards in his career, and Cook currently has 4,966, so Allen needs nine yards against the Vikings and Cook needs 34 yards to reach 5,000.

Allen is averaging 39 rushing yards per game this season and Cook is averaging 101, so it’s likely that they’ll both reach the 5,000-yard milestone on Monday night.

Allen would be the fifth quarterback in NFL history with 5,000 career rushing yards. Ravens quarterback Lamar Jackson is the NFL’s all-time quarterback leader with 6,666 career rushing yards. Behind Jackson are Michael Vick with 6,109, Cam Newton with 5,628 and Russell Wilson with 5,568. Allen probably won’t catch Jackson, who, though currently injured, is a year younger and will keep adding to his yardage total. But the 30-year-old Allen has a great chance of continuing to rack up rushing yards long enough to move ahead of Vick into No. 2 in rushing yardage among quarterbacks in NFL history.

Cook is in his fifth year in the NFL and is on closing in on his fourth consecutive 1,000-yard season. He ranks 15th among active NFL players in career rushing yards, and Allen ranks 14th.

#2789. 3 takeaways as the Mavericks’ comeback comes up just short, 112-111, at the San Antonio Spurs

The Dallas Mavericks (4-4) nearly pulled off a ridiculous comeback Wednesday night, but fell 112-111 to the San Antonio Spurs (6-2) after a strange final possession. Victor Wembanyama completely dominated the game, finishing with 52 points, 24 rebounds, and eight blocks while controlling everything Dallas tried to do around the rim. Kyrie Irving led the Mavericks with 29 points, while Cooper Flagg recovered from a brutal first half to finish with 19 points, 10 rebounds and five assists. Naji Marshall was huge off the bench with 22 points on 9-of-12 shooting, helping Flagg lead a second-half comeback that gave Dallas a chance to win on the final possession.

The Mavericks had a rough opening quarter in San Antonio, mostly because Victor Wembanyama looked completely in control while Dallas' two best players could not get anything going. Wembanyama had 15 points, eight rebounds, three steals and two blocks in just over eight minutes, while Cooper Flagg missed all seven of his shots and Kyrie Irving started 2-of-8. Morez Johnson Jr. gave Dallas some good energy off the bench, but the Mavericks shot just 31 percent and struggled to finish anything around the rim. San Antonio led 32-26 after one.

The second quarter made the matchup look even worse. Wembanyama completely erased the paint, forcing hesitations, kick-outs, and bad attempts while blocking Flagg, P.J. Washington, and Daniel Gafford in the same stretch. By halftime, he already had 29 points, 15 rebounds, and five blocks. Flagg was just 1-of-11 with four points and no assists; Kyrie had 17, and San Antonio dominated the glass 44-31 with 15 offensive rebounds. Dallas trailed 68-51 and looked completely overmatched.

The Mavericks finally showed some life in the third. They won the non-Wembanyama minutes, Flagg started to look more aggressive, and the small-ball approach gave San Antonio more problems. Kyrie helped push the comeback, Walter Clayton Jr. hit another three, and Dallas won the quarter 29-22 to cut the deficit to 90-80. Wembanyama was still everywhere and finished with 40 points, but Dallas had at least made the game competitive again.

The fourth quarter was easily Dallas' best stretch. Naji Marshall and Flagg led the comeback, with Marshall hitting huge shots and Flagg finally getting downhill and creating offense. Dallas sped the game up, went small, and did about as good a job as possible neutralizing Wembanyama, though he still made several massive plays late. Marshall's three with 1:41 left tied the game at 111, and after Wembanyama split a pair of free throws with 24 seconds left, Dallas had one final chance to win. The possession went nowhere, ending with a difficult Kyrie turnaround fadeaway with three seconds left, and the Mavericks fell 112-111.

Cooper Flagg was awful in the first half, and aside from Victor Wembanyama completely taking over, he was probably the biggest reason Dallas got buried early. Flagg went just 1-of-11 before halftime, could not get to his spots, struggled badly against San Antonio's length, and started passing up shots he normally takes. He also didn't give Dallas enough defensively, which made the performance feel even worse. The second half was completely different. Flagg finally started attacking, got out in transition, made better reads, and became one of the main reasons Dallas even had a chance to win. He finished with 19 points, 10 rebounds, and five assists, and while the 7-of-19 shooting line still wasn't pretty, most of the damage came after halftime. He and Naji Marshall led the comeback, and Flagg looked much more like the player Dallas needs him to be down the stretch. The first half was probably his worst stretch of the season, but the response mattered.

Dallas had the ball down one with 24 seconds left and a chance to win the game, and the final possession was baffling. The Mavericks waited until roughly 10 seconds remained to really initiate anything, then basically just handed the ball to Kyrie Irving and asked him to make something happen. No screen, no dribble handoff, no action to force a switch, no attempt to get Flagg involved, just a Kyrie isolation that ended in a difficult turnaround fadeaway with three seconds left. It felt like one of those old Jason Kidd end-of-game possessions where the entire offense disappears, and the plan becomes "Kyrie, go save us." That cannot be the best option. Kyrie is obviously one of the best isolation scorers in basketball, but when you have an entire timeout to draw something up, you have to make the defense work harder than that. Dusty May has been creative offensively in plenty of situations already, which made this even stranger. Dallas had a chance to steal a game after being down big, and the final possession did not give them nearly enough of a chance.

There's really no more complicated way to say it. Wembanyama was incredible.

He finished with 52 points, 24 rebounds, and eight blocks on 16-of-28 shooting, while also getting to the free-throw line 23 times. The numbers are absurd, but his impact on the game was even bigger. Dallas could not operate normally offensively because every paint touch became a problem. Drivers hesitated, bigs had shots erased, and the Mavericks were constantly forced into kick-outs or difficult attempts because Wembanyama was waiting around the rim.

Dallas did a much better job neutralizing him in the second half by playing smaller, speeding up the game, and making him defend in space, but he still found ways to dominate. He hit a huge three in the fourth, finished possessions on the glass, and scored the free throw that ultimately gave San Antonio the winning point. This was one of those games where you walk away understanding exactly why Wembanyama changes everything. Dallas nearly stole it anyway, but for most of the night, he completely dictated what the Mavericks were allowed to do.
