#2787. Sean Payton says J.K. Dobbins remains "a huge part of what we're doing"

It’s been a somewhat strange second year in Denver for veteran running back J.K. Dobbins. As coach Sean Payton tells it, however, everything is going as planned.

“He’s a huge part of what we’re doing,” Payton told reporters on Wednesday regarding whether the team is managing Dobbins’s workload. “So each week we look at — a lot of times who’s the back that’s in there with the hot hand. But he’s been fantastic. So to answer your question: No, that’s not a hot button topic with us here. It might be with you guys, but not with us. So we’re good. We’re good with the rotation.”

Payton is generally using a three-back rotation, with Dobbins joining R.J. Harvey and rookie Jonah Coleman. Still, with Harvey on injured reserve for Sunday’s showdown against the Chiefs, Dobbins got fewer chances than Coleman.

Coleman, who was on the field for 41 offensive plays, had 11 carries for 41 yards and four catches for 63. Dobbins played 13 snaps, getting seven carries for 13 yards and no targets in the passing game.

“Look, it’s always easy to work two [running backs] and it becomes more challenging when you’re trying to work three, but he’s doing a great job,” Payton said of Dobbins.

For the year, Dobbins has 94 carries for 306 yards in eight games, with eight catches for 27 yards. That’s 333 yards from scrimmage — an average of 41.6 per game.

In 10 games last year, before he suffered a season-ending foot injury during a Thursday night game against the Raiders, Dobbins was averaging nearly twice that amount, at 80.9 yards from scrimmage per game.

Through it all, the Broncos have been linked to a potential trade for Colts running back Jonathan Taylor. While the prospect of acquiring a workhorse would cut against Payton’s longstanding approach to use multiple running backs, Taylor’s arrival would surely result in even fewer chances for Dobbins.

#2786. Zac Taylor gives first impression of Madrid ahead of Bengals practice

MADRID, SPAIN – The Cincinnati Bengals (5-2) have arrived in Spain and are preparing to face the Atlanta Falcons (3-5) on Nov. 8 at the world-famous Santiago Bernabéu Stadium.

Zac Taylor is in his eighth season as the Bengals head coach and has only taken his team overseas one other time back in 2019 when Cincinnati played the Los Angeles Rams in London at Wembley Stadium and lost.

Taylor spoke head of practice at the Real Federación Española de Fútbol (RFEF) and offered his first impressions of Madrid.

"We've been working a lot," Taylor said. "I think the players have probably gotten out a little bit more. But we came over here yesterday and just walked around the facility. Pretty neat, beautiful city from what I've seen so far. Look forward to experiencing it a little bit more over the next couple days."

The RFEF training facility serves as the home for the Spanish national soccer team. After he arrived in Spain, Taylor came over to the practice facility a day before practice to learn his new whereabouts.

Taylor was hoping to see the FIFA World Cup trophy at the RFEF as Spain is the reigning World Cup champions, but learned the trophy is working its way around Spain currently.

"I was here yesterday looking for it," Taylor said. "It's not here. It's traveling around Spain. I learned that. It's on a whole tour of Spain, but I did my best to find it. I know it's a big soccer country. That's their number one sport. I'm not quite sure how much they know about our game yet. Hopefully, they'll learn a lot over the course of this week. It's a fun one."

The Bengals traveled through the night on Nov. 3 and arrived in Spain in the morning on Nov. 4. Taylor gave his players the day off when they arrived, with practice scheduled for Nov. 5 and 6. Select players, including Joe Burrow, Tee Higgins, Ja'Marr Chase, Dexter Lawrence, Chase Brown, Ted Karras and Jonathan Allen will all speak to the media over the course of the next two days in Madrid.

Taylor says the team is back on schedule now that they're here. It was important to Taylor to get his team to Spain early enough in the week so that their bodies could adjust to the time difference. Spain is six hours ahead of Cincinnati time wise.

"I think this is the best compromise we found to make sure that we can get acclimated by Friday, get a really good practice where we feel better, and then play our best on Sunday," Taylor said. "We've all embraced that mindset, and I think it's working well for us so far."

The Bengals will hold a walk-through at Santiago Bernabéu Stadium on Nov. 7, the day before the game against the Falcons. Bernabéu is the second-largest stadium (83,186 seats) in Europe and is the home stadium of Real Madrid.

"I know the tradition of soccer here is unbelievable," Taylor said. "People who follow it are very passionate. I think to be able to be in a stadium where there's so much history with the team is cool for our guys to have a chance to see a stadium like that with the tradition of soccer has. We'll embrace and enjoy it."

#2785. Broncos proactively replace entire surface at Mile High Stadium, again

With four regular-season home games played and four to go, the Broncos are being proactive — again — about the quality of the playing surface at Mile High Stadium.

The entire field is being ripped up and replaced, despite the absence of any complaints about the quality of the grass there.

For the fifth straight year, the Broncos are spending the money to ensure that the players will be performing on the highest-quality surface, emphasizing that “the Walton Penner Family Ownership Group’s commitment to player safety and a best-in-class playing surface throughout the season.”

At a time when the debate regarding real grass vs. fake grass continues, with the situation boiling down to whether the owners are willing to write the check to ensure the best and safest surfaces for players, the statement made by the Broncos makes their ownership look good and, in comparison, owners who cling to artificial turf look bad.

Beyond caring about player safety, having the best playing surface provides the best protection of the investment the owners have made in their rosters. Which would be a sensible position for any owner — especially the cheap ones.

Now that it has morphed into a matter of collective bargaining, those who choose to be pennywise have even more cover for their pound foolishness. Which makes it even more important that the NFL Players Association apply not general public pressure to the league but specific scrutiny to the owners who won’t ditch artificial turf for grass, or who won’t replace low-quality grass with high-quality grass.

#2784. Lamar Jackson's latest injury raises obvious questions about his future in Baltimore

With quarterback Lamar Jackson’s ninth NFL season possibly over after three full games and two first-half exits, obvious questions have emerged regarding his future in Baltimore.

The facts fuel the speculation. He’s under contract for one more season, and the Ravens can’t use the franchise tag or the transition tag to limit his ability to become an unrestricted free agent in March 2028, which is only 16 months away.

If Jackson wants a fresh start at age 31, he’ll be able to have one.

The Ravens made it clear in January that they wanted to extend his contract by the start of the new league year in March 2026. It didn’t happen, for reasons that never became clear because neither Jackson nor the Ravens (at Jackson’s behest) share information about the negotiations.

Before the season began, it seemed that a new contract wa just a matter of time. The Ravens surely would like to do it before the start of the new league year in March, when Jackson’s cap number spikes to $84.34 million. Although the team has the right to do another restructuring that would reduce the 2027 cap number, that would make the dead-cap reckoning even larger as of 2028.

A trade would avoid the final $52 million in cash and cap charges, but the cap realities would make a post-June 1 move the far better option. And there have been whispers of at least one team doing advance homework on a potential pursuit of Jackson in 2027.

The overriding question is whether Jackson’s lingering availability issue changes things for the Ravens. For now, there’s no reason to think it has. When the dust settles on the season, the Ravens will have to revisit that question.

But that will lead to another question. What would they do at quarterback without Lamar Jackson? That simple reality prompted them to give him a market-level deal in 2023, and to want to do it again.

As long as that desire to avoid a future without Lamar Jackson remains, there’s no reason to think he won’t be back in Baltimore in 2027.

#2783. Steelers trade targets: Watch Josh Downs, Brian Thomas Jr. before NFL deadline

The list of glaring needs for Pittsburgh Steelers general manager Omar Khan ahead of the NFL trade deadline on Nov. 10 is remarkably short.

The offensive line, which has been a franchise project for years, has come together nicely since guard Brock Hoffman and rookie tackle Max Iheanachor were installed on the right side starting in Week 3. The offense has depth at running back, quarterback and tight end.

The defensive front seven is swallowing opposing running games whole at the moment. The Cleveland Browns and New Orleans Saints have totaled just 52 rushing yards total over the past two games. And the defensive secondary has been containing explosive pass plays thanks to first-year coordinator Patrick Graham's zone coverage schemes.

Required reading: Aaron Rodgers hasn't been very efficient in Steelers' 4-game winning streak

Of course, adding star power at any of those position groups could help. In terms of tangible weaknesses, however, the receiver position stands out as the one place where this team is clearly deficient right now.

Injuries are the No. 1 reason. Key offseason acquisition Michael Pittman Jr. has appeared in just three games and made limited impact because of a foot injury. Former third-round draft pick Roman Wilson has also been on the proverbial shelf for several weeks with a finger injury.

The latter still has fewer than 400 yards in his career, now in his third season, so it's not clear he could make a significant impact consistently even if he were healthy.

Veteran DK Metcalf, meanwhile, has been mostly ineffective as the team's top receiver. He's had 40 or fewer yards in five of his eight games this season. Only one receiver in football has more than his six drops. His contested-catch percentage of 39.1% ranks 17th among 21 receivers with at least 50 targets in 2026, per Pro Football Focus data.

Second-round draft pick Germie Bernard has shown some positive signs with 284 yards and a touchdown to open his first NFL season, but he has not yet developed as a meaningful downfield threat. His average depth of target (ADOT) is just 4.9 yards.

The Steelers, therefore, have a clear mandate for change at this position, should Khan be willing to part with NFL draft capital to acquire it. Here, USA TODAY Sports looks at potential trade targets and why they do - or don't make sense.

TRADE DEADLINE: NFL trade candidates include Derrick Henry and another Jets surprise

ESPN's Dan Graziano linked the Steelers to the fourth-year veteran in a report Wednesday morning. The Colts are 2-6 and look like clear sellers, and Downs is nearing the end of his rookie deal, which should make his price manageable.

The upside in his statistical profile is clear. His ADOT is 10.3 yards, which has allowed him to threaten parts of the field that Bernard has not as the team's No. 2. With 330 total receiving yards, he's only been marginally less productive than DK Metcalf, who has 378.

There's reason to be concerned that his skill set overlaps with Wilson's. Both are smaller receivers who work primarily out of the slot and rely on separation to make plays.

The Steelers can't wait on Wilson's development, though, as they sit in first place in the AFC North. If they can acquire a more proven slot option for a reasonable price, then that makes them better, whether Wilson is healthy or not.

The 2024 first-round pick just hasn't fit in coach Liam Cohen's offense. His numbers have dropped precipitously from 1,282 yards and 10 touchdowns as a rookie to 707 yards and two scores upon Cohen's arrival in 2025, and to 10 catches for 117 yards and two touchdowns this season. Trade rumors have swirled around him as a result.

He offers more size than Downs at 6-2. And at his best as a rookie, his ADOT was a robust 11.9 yards.

First-year coach Mike McCarthy would need to be confident that a change of scenery could yield immediate results. The Steelers already have enough headaches with Metcalf. They don't need a second project if they have productive names available.

The Jets star is one of the few names Khan could acquire with the clear intent to surpass Metcalf on the depth chart. He's been a 1,000-yard receiver in each of his three healthy seasons. And he has 43 catches for 527 yards and three touchdowns in 2026.

Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers was his signal caller for two of those productive seasons in New York, so there's pre-existing chemistry to potentially be mined.

The Jets have him under contract through 2030, so there's no clear need to move him, even in the midst of an abysmal 2-6 start. The Steelers would probably have to present an offer Darren Mougey could not refuse to get something done. It's questionable whether that's worthwhile for the Steelers with Metcalf under contract and uncertainty at quarterback after Rodgers retires at the end of the year.

The former Heisman Trophy winner is another good receiver on a 2-6 team that's going nowhere this year. He's more affordable than Garrett Wilson, with only two years left on his deal at a reasonable rate. He's been productive with 310 yards and two touchdowns in just four games. He's also a true downfield threat, with a career ADOT of 13.6 yards.

The four games are the problem. He's battled a hamstring injury this year, so Khan may not want to add more potential issues to the ones he already has with Pittman and Roman Wilson.

This 24-year-old should simply cost too much for the Steelers. Unlike Thomas, he's remained productive, even as the Chargers are 0-7. He's averaging 16.8 yards per catch in 2026 and a highly efficient 2.23 yards per route run.

For those reasons, Los Angeles would likely prefer to give him a nice contract extension than give him up to the Steelers for anything less than a proverbial mint. And the Steelers aren't the franchise that traditionally overpays to get what it wants.

As former coach Mike Tomlin once said: Never say never, but never.

#2782. Lakers win uneven game over Kings behind 40 points from Luka Doncic

On a night when Lakers coach JJ Redick said his team was "a little flat," Luka Doncic flattened yet another opponent.

Even Doncic started slow compared to his usual first-quarter exploits, but he picked up his pace as the game progressed, dropping 40 points on the woeful Sacramento Kings to lead the Lakers to a 116-103 win Wednesday night at Golden 1 Center.

Doncic has scored 40-plus points in three straight games and in five of his last six.

So, after shooting 11 for 23 from the field and six for 13 from three-point range while he also notched nine rebounds and seven assists, Doncic was asked if he's ever had a better offensive stretch over his eight-year NBA career.

Read more: Fun, flowing, not yet flawless: Lakers' league-best offense still has room to improve

"Maybe. I don't know," he said. "I had some good stretches in my career. But obviously this could be one of the highest ones. But there's still some work to do."

Doncic had 10 points in the first quarter, a slow start for him considering he averages 15 points per game in the first 12 minutes. He had 13 in the second, 12 in the third and five in the fourth.

He even made a 360-degree three-pointer in the third.

"He's playing great right now and he's doing a great job," Redick said. "We talked about this after the game or before the game, but he's doing a great job just playing off the ball. We're trying to set off-ball screens for him. Other guys are handling (the ball). So, I think some of that workload from bringing the ball up against pressure every single possession. Like it's just not there right now, and that's very intentional on our part."

In the middle of all of this, Doncic is making history.

He became the first player in NBA history to record six consecutive games with 35-plus points, five-plus rebounds, five-plus assists and three-plus three-pointers.

The season is just two weeks old and Doncic is dominating in ways not seen very often.

When asked if he was in midseason form, Doncic shrugged.

"I don't know, honestly," he said. "Too early to tell, you know. But as I go back, I had the whole summer to recover. A lot of stuff that I couldn't do in the last maybe eight years. So that's where the energy is coming from."

Walker Kessler had a strong game with 15 points on six-for-eight shooting, eight rebounds and three blocks to aid Doncic.

Read more: Lakers newsletter: Luka Doncic's scoring reaches new universe

Austin Reaves had 21 points to help Doncic out against a Kings team that is tied with four other teams with the worst record in the league at 1-7.

They give up 124.3 points per game, the second-most in the league and teams shoot 50.5% against them, a league-high.

So, the high-scoring Lakers just had to play to their usual effort.

They began the game second in scoring (122.5) in the league and first in field-goal percentage (52%).

But the first half was a choppy affair because of all the fouls being called.

Each team was called for 12 fouls in the first half. The Lakers were called for nine fouls in the second quarter and the Kings were called for eight.

Jake LaRavia picked up his fourth foul with eight minutes and two seconds left in the second quarter.

The Lakers had committed enough fouls to put the Kings in the penalty with 9:24 left in the second quarter.

That was the kind of first half the Lakers had to endure.

But when Doncic got going in the second quarter, the Lakers played a little better.

He scored 13 of their final 15 points in the second quarter and finished the first half with 23 points.

Still, Doncic took the blame for the Lakers' lackadaisical start.

"Yeah, that was on me. I came out little sloppy. I take responsibility for that," Doncic said. "I know that my first quarter wasn't good. So I just came back in the game trying to be more aggressive, be more focused."

#2781. Glacier spikers get past Butte in 5 sets, make State

It's not about how you start, but how you finish.

Glacier had both going its way in a Western AA volleyball playoff victory over Butte, but the third and fourth sets left the Wolfpack with work to do in the 5-set victory at the Wolf Den Wednesday evening.

"I don't know why we have to go to five with Butte every single time," Glacier coach Jaimie Nelson said. "I am proud of my girls, there were a couple moments where they could have just let it slip away, but they decided to fight instead."

After splitting the first four sets, Glacier commanded the fifth set to take the victory and secure its spot at the State AA Volleyball tournament in Bozeman Nov. 12-14.

Allie Krueger opened the final set with a kill after the Pack scrambled to get the ball over the net earlier in the rally.

Then, Glacier added four kills split between Krueger and Kyla Gully to go up 6-0.

Butte earned two points on long serves from Glacier, but the Wolfpack had an instant answer each time. Madi Stevens served up back-to-back aces to help Glacier lead 14-2.

Cadence Graham sparked a little life into the Bulldogs with four straight points, but Glacier closed out the match with a 15-6 win in the fifth set.

Nelson said this may have been the most dominant set she has seen this team play.

"I don't remember one off the top of my head," Nelson said. "I think that was pretty much them saying, 'We are here to go and do what we have to do to get to our goal.' "

The start was just what Glacier was looking for also as the Pack sparked a run off of a Stevens ace to go up 16-13 and take set one 25-19.

That momentum continued into set two where Glacier jumped out to a quick 9-2 lead after Audrey Mitchell served an ace. Butte closed to 14-9 later in the set but got no closer as the Wolfpack took set two 25-17.

Set three is where Butte found its footing.

The Pack led 11-7 in the set when Elli Graham stepped up to serve. She guided the Bulldogs to 11 straight points and an 18-12 lead. They continued the run to win the set 25-14 and force set four.

Glacier had more early momentum in the fourth set, but again Butte had a rally. Stevens put Glacier up 15-8, then the Bulldogs scored four of the next five points.

Butte eventually tied the set at 19 and then used a Cadence Graham kill to take a 22-21 lead.

Glacier wasn't done though as they battled back from 24-21 down to extend the set thanks to a kill from Krueger.

The teams went back and forth before Butte sealed the win 30-28 with a kill from Avery Barsness tie the match at two and set up the deciding set.

"I felt like we could have done it a little cleaner and taken advantage where we could have," Nelson said. "But to take the momentum into the fifth with them and close it out, I was proud of that."

Glacier moves to 11-8 on the season with the win. Butte finishes the year 8-12.

Butte's statistics were not made available.

Glacier def. Butte 25-19, 25-17, 14-25, 28-30, 15-6

Aces — Glacier 10 (Madi Stevens 3, Audrey Mitchell 3). Kills — Glacier 67 (Allie Krueger 20, Kyla Gully 16). Assists — Glacier 53 (Stevens 51, Addison Thramer 2). Blocks — Glacier 7 (Chloe Farrell 4). Digs — Glacier 85 (Thramer 22, Aria Stewart 19).

#2780. Saints WR Jordyn Tyson feels "more explosive than I ever have" in return from hamstring injury

The Saints can use all the help they can get after a 2-5 start to the season and one ray of hope is the return of rookie wide receiver Jordyn Tyson to the practice field this week.

Tyson has been out since injuring his hamstring during a joint practice with the Jaguars in August, but the first-round pick was designated for return from injured reserve this week and he gave a very positive assessment of his health while speaking with reporters on Wednesday.

“I ran the fastest I ran since I been here in rehab. I feel more explosive than I ever have,” Tyson said. “So I think I’m doing pretty good. I think I’m doing just fine.”

The Saints haven’t said if Tyson will play against the Browns this Sunday, but he said he’s “pretty anxious” to make his NFL debut and start providing the big plays that the team envisioned when they took him eighth overall in April. That would be a positive way to head into the second half of a season that has not gone as hoped in New Orleans.

#2778. The Jets will have the last laugh on the Colts

As this season continues to spiral, the effects are currently being felt. All of the losing has cost the Indianapolis Colts two of their franchise pillars. More could fall soon. The losing is taking its toll on fans and players alike. Sometimes there is a silver lining, though. The good thing is that it's true in this case. The bad thing is that silver lining belongs to the New York Jets.

Two first-round picks were surrendered for Sauce Gardner. Two. The first one was felt as the Colts dropped from Super Bowl contention and into the middle of the draft. That is pain most can live with. It's this year's lingering pain that has carried over and is making this dreadful season that much worse to watch. Instead of the Colts anticipating a potential top-ten pick in the first round of the draft, the Jets are sitting pretty at fourth overall.

You can't have a rainbow without the rain, and sometimes there is a pot of gold at the end of that rainbow. That isn't the case for the Colts this year. Normally, pain is rewarded with a great opportunity to start fresh, gather new cornerstones to build your franchise out of the ashes. Yes, the Colts, with whatever horrific record they finish, will still have good positioning in subsequent rounds, but that lack of a first-round selection could haunt them.

Let's not even talk about the return. As good as Gardner can be, he has missed way too much time in his short stint with the Colts to be deemed worthy of the trade. Oh, and what did the Colts throw in at the end? Adonai Mitchell. He seems to be having a bit of a resurgence after getting into Shane Steichen's doghouse and being a throw away piece. Seeing any success he has is also a tough watch.

These are the stings that can stick with a franchise for a long time. If it all holds, not having the fourth overall pick is going to make some people sick. It has already cost some their jobs. That will only compound the issue. If the Jets select a Hall of Fame player with that selection, look out. This is the state of the Colts, and the Jets will be laughing all the way to the bank

#2777. Nick Sirianni: I've always felt complete support from Jeffrey Lurie

Nick Sirianni has never missed the playoffs since becoming the Eagles’ head coach and he’s won one of the two Super Bowls the team has played in during his tenure, but the waters have gotten rockier for him over the last 12 months.

The Eagles will bring a six-game losing streak into Sunday’s game against the Giants and the team is 5-11 since an 8-2 start to the 2025 season. While his overall history and the overall circumstances of this season would say that he’s earned a chance to turn things around, Eagles history says that team owner Jeffrey Lurie hasn’t shied away from making changes after a season goes awry.

Doug Pederson also won a Super Bowl for the Eagles, but was dismissed after snapping a three-year postseason run by going 4-11-1 in 2020. That may have factored into a question for Sirianni on Wednesday about his communications with Lurie during the team’s current difficulties.

“I’ve always felt nothing but complete support from Mr. Lurie in everything, through good times, through bad times,” Sirianni said, via a transcript from the team. “That’s huge. That’s huge to be able to know that the owner has your back in all situations. We’ve been high of highs, we’ve been low, and I’ve felt nothing but support and my communication remains the same with him as it has [been] whether we’re on a winning streak or whether we’re on a losing streak. I love that steadiness, and I’m trying to give that same thing to the guys: the consistency, the steadiness, because I know I’m receiving it from the very top.”

Sirianni spoke before word broke that the Eagles will veer away from steadiness at quarterback this week. They’ll give Joe Milton a chance to run the offense well enough to snap a skid that will certainly impact Sirianni’s job security if it doesn’t come to an end relatively soon.

#2776. Sam Darnold out Week 9 with quad injury, Drew Lock in line to start

Quarterback Sam Darnold will not play in Sunday’s game against the Cardinals after suffering a quad injury late in Monday’s loss to the Bears, Seahawks head coach Mike Macdonald announced in his Wednesday press conference.

“It’ll be week-to-week for Sam,” Macdonald said. “He’s not going to go on IR.”

Macdonald noted the club intends to start Drew Lock on Sunday, but he’s also working through an injury.

“The plan is for Drew to start. Jalen [Milroe] will be ready to back up,” Macdonald said. “Drew’s still working back from his elbow, so we’ll work through that process this week. So we’ll be getting both guys ready to play. Have full confidence in those guys and we have a plan in place and we’ll go execute.”

Lock finished the Week 1 win over the Patriots and started Week 2 when the Seahawks beat the Cardinals in Arizona. He’s completed 35-of-48 passes this year for 422 yards with four touchdowns and no interceptions.

“He’s able to throw. How much, we’re working through that right now. That’s the best way to put it,” Macdonald said of Lock’s elbow injury. “He’s going to throw the ball throughout the week, but we’re just going to manage it. He’s not going to take 8,000 throws.”

Lock and Milroe are set to split reps at least early in the practice week.

“I think we just have to take it day-by-day at this point,” Macdonald said.

While Macdonald characterized Darnold as week-to-week with the quad injury, the quarterback is also dealing with another issue.

“In terms of Sam, this guy, he’s tough as nails,” Macdonald said. “I think the second play of the game, I just asked if I could share this, but he cracked his rib on the second play of the game. So, playing the whole game without even making a name of it, and playing his tail off, and competing, it’s worth noting how tough this guy is. He’ll be back sooner than later, I’m sure.”

Darnold has completed 60.2 percent of his passes this season for 1,478 yards with 10 touchdowns and nine interceptions so far this season.

Seattle’s first injury report of the week will be out later on Wednesday.

#2774. Eagles’ new QB taught teammate a hard lesson: ‘Don’t tell (him) I said that’

PHILADELPHIA — Eagles wide receiver Darius Cooper knows from now on that he must wear gloves when catching passes from new starting quarterback Joe Milton.

Milton throws harder than most NFL quarterbacks, and Cooper wants to protect his hands.

During the 2024 NFL Combine, Milton tied Bills quarterback Josh Allen's combine record for the fastest throw ever recorded at 62 miles per hour.

"I would say I have pretty rough, sturdy hands," Cooper said on Wednesday. "But today during walkthrough, I ain't had no gloves on. Stung a little bit. Just a little bit. Don't tell [Joe] I said that."

Milton will become the third Eagles quarterback to start a game this season. Jalen Hurts started the first five games before being placed on injured reserve after blood clots were discovered in his lungs. Fourth-year backup Tanner McKee replaced Hurts as the starter for three games.

On Wednesday, three weeks after signing Milton off the Cowboys' practice squad, the Eagles named him their new starting quarterback. They benched McKee after he struggled in his first three starts, completing 72 of 114 passes for 638 yards, two touchdowns and two interceptions.

With the Eagles having lost six in a row, Milton is unlikely to save their season. He might not even be an upgrade over McKee, but the Eagles are making this change because they are desperate for a spark.

"Have you seen the guy's arm? It is a f—ing cannon," Eagles offensive tackle Jordan Mailata said. "Oh, my god. Pardon my language. You see it on tv, you hear about it when he was going through the draft, but then when you see it, it's a work of art, man."

The Eagles dropped to 2-6 after a 27-10 loss to the Washington Commanders last Sunday. McKee struggled for the third consecutive week to handle pressure and to make plays out of structure. The Commanders sacked McKee five times for a loss of 35 yards and intercepted one of his passes.

With Philadelphia's offensive line struggling in pass protection, the Eagles need Milton to extend plays with his legs and make creative throws outside the pocket to beat the New York Giants on Sunday.

"That's beyond me," Eagles tight end Dallas Goedert said about the team's decision to switch quarterbacks. "Obviously feel for Tanner in this situation. I don't think he played terrible, but I think they're trying to do anything to find a spark.

"It'd be nice if it wasn't out there and we could surprise them late in the week and maybe they panic a little bit. With his skill set, he brings something different to the table than Tanner did with his mobility. So we'll see how that works on Sunday."

A sixth-round pick of the New England Patriots in 2024, Milton has a starter-caliber arm, but his accuracy and decision-making are inconsistent.

The Patriots traded him to the Dallas Cowboys in 2025 for a fifth-round pick. One year later, Dallas waived him before the start of the 2026 season.

Milton will make his first NFL start against the Giants, but he has played in five games over the last two years. In those games, he completed 37 of his 53 passes for 424 yards and two touchdowns, and he recorded 66 rushing yards and one rushing touchdown.

Josh Uche has pretty much defined serviceable this season.

He might not be keeping offensive tackles awake at night, but he generally does his job.

On a misdirection run, much of the defense followed Corey Kiner's jet motion. Uche stayed home and was able to corral Rhamondre Stevenson. He also finished with four tackles and a third-down sack that dropped Maye for a 10-yard loss.

Chop Robinson added two sacks and showed some versatility beyond rushing the passer. On third-and-5 with 9:22 left in the first quarter, he bluffed a rush before dropping into the middle of the field, helping take away an option as Maye threw incomplete.

Robinson also had a chance to bring Maye down before DeMario Douglas' 48-yard touchdown and couldn't finish it.

#2770. Stats Rundown: 3 numbers to know as the Mavericks drop 112-111 heartbreaker at the San Antonio Spurs

The Dallas Mavericks (4-4) fell to the San Antonio Spurs (6-2), 112-111, in a nationally televised matchup on the road on Wednesday. The two squads met for the second time, and it came after the Mavericks' 115-100 blunder against the Sacramento Kings on Monday. The matchup went down to the wire after the Mavericks were able to turn around a 19-point deficit.

Santi Aldama, Tarik Biberovic, Max Christie, Sergio de Larrea, and Dereck Lively were out for the Mavericks. Tobias Harris was out for the Spurs.

Kyrie Irving led the Mavericks with 29 points in the loss. PJ Washington added 21 points and 10 rebounds. Victor Wembanyama had an otherworldly 52 points, 24 rebounds, eight blocks, and two steals.

Here are three numbers to know from Wednesday night's clutch loss.

PJ Washington and Naji Marshall left their mark on the game, finishing with a combined 43 points. Washington finished with 21 points and added 10 rebounds, including four offensive boards. He has been the Mavericks' best rebounder through the start of the season and was a boost to the Mavericks on the glass despite the team losing the rebounding battle to the Spurs.

Marshall contributed 22 points, with 17 of them coming in the second half as the Mavericks closed the gap on their 19-point deficit to the Spurs. It was a bounce-back game for him after a performance to forget in Monday night's loss, after returning from an illness. The Mavericks needed role players to step up as Cooper Flagg struggled early, and the forward pairing was able to answer the call to keep the Mavericks competitive despite the loss.

Kyrie Irving finished with 29 points, 7 rebounds, and 5 assists. 17 of his points came in the first half, keeping the Mavericks within reach of the game when Cooper Flagg struggled early. The Mavericks rested Irving Monday night due to knee injury management to have him ready for the matchup with San Antonio, and his early scoring was key to the Mavericks staying within reach of the game. Though his shots didn't fall late, Kyrie Irving is critical to the Mavericks' offense, allowing them to compete with some of the league's best on any given night.

Cooper Flagg's Monday night struggles flowed into Wednesday night's performance. He started the game 1-of-11 in the first half, with a questionable shot diet that only worsened his offensive struggles early. He came into the second half looking like the Cooper Flagg we know and love, and finished the second half six-of-eight. The Mavericks need Flagg to continue to play with the aggression he showed in the second half. His ability to shake off his early performance proves that he has the ability to be a star in the league. When Flagg got going, the Mavericks were able to dig themselves out of the hole they were in and have a fighting chance.

#2769. Full Count: Valkyries want to take the next leap

In Ariel Putnam's fourth season as Bigfork's volleyball coach, the Valkyries reached a landmark: The 2022 State B tournament. It was their first state appearance in 17 years.

Year 8 could bring another milestone. After reaching the State A in 2024, the Vals want to return this month and stay a couple days at Bozeman's Brick Breeden Fieldhouse.

State is always the goal, but building confidence in tough situations became a renewed priority this fall.

"Last year we had a very talented team, but every time we got into these very tough situations, we didn't know how to handle them," Putnam said. "We've really worked on it every day, putting ourselves in a tough situation in practice. We reward effort, and we're OK with an error."

Bigfork's junior-laden squad won 28 matches in 2025 before faltering at the Western A Divisional. Now senior-laden, the Vals went 11-1 in Northwest A play for a second straight season and are playing Corvallis to start this year's divisional on Thursday.

"The last two years we've had a couple key players here and there that we've lost," Putnam said. "But for three of my senior hitters, this is their third year on varsity."

Outside hitters Sofia Lowell, a junior, and Raegen Waller, a senior, never leave the rotation. Seniors Somer Campos and Lillie Suffia are the middle blockers.

Junior Payton Despain is the Vals' 6-foot setter; junior Kenley Wheeler plays libero. Seniors Olivia Carson and Emily Wisman are the defensive specialist and right-side hitter, respectively.

The squad cruised until Butte's Blocktober Tournament, finishing second in its pool before going 1-2 in bracket play with losses to Columbia Falls and Hamilton — a callback to 2025.

"Last year we were in the same situation," Putnam said. "We played really tough volleyball, and played well, but we lacked this confidence. They were playing a little behind the pace of play."

So the Valkyries had to re-regroup — and did, winning their next four matches without dropping a set. But there were tests.

In a key match at Columbia Falls on Oct. 27, Bigfork trailed 25-24 in the first set and 24-22 in the third. The Vals won both 27-25, with a 25-17 win in between.

"We've had the talent; what we've been working on is fostering an environment where the girls controlling their game," Putnam said. "How are we handling the huddle; how are we using our breath and how are we holding our heads high for our teammates?"

Campos had 10 digs at C-Falls; Lowell had eight. Campos hits a .334 percentage.

Add it up and the Valkyries have a No. 1 seed going to the Western A.

"I don't have one girl that I don't have full trust in get the job done," she said. "I feel very fortunate. They're very professional, they show up and they're very serious about volleyball."

#2768. Patriots opponent preview: Packers are facing injury questions of their own

After back-to-back road games, the New England Patriots will be back at Gillette Stadium this week to take on a Green Bay Packers team that has played some successful football so far this season. At 5-3, they are currently in the NFC playoff picture and have shown themselves capable of winning both at home and on the road.

What the Packers also have shown is that they are capable of winning despite facing serious personnel questions. Much like the Patriots, they have been hit hard and will be without starters or key reserves at wide receiver, along the offensive line, along the defensive line and at linebacker this Sunday.

So, what can be expected in Week 9? Let's find out.

The Packers are a good football team, they just happen to play in what is the most competitive division in football right now. Despite a 5-3 record, they are in fourth place in the NFC North; they are, however, the current owners of the seventh playoff seed in the conference — same as their opponent this week, the Patriots.

And that is not the only similarity between the two teams as a look at the key stats shows.

Offensively, the Packers function mainly due to their passing game. They are ranked top-10 in attempts, yards, touchdowns and net yard per attempt; they barely rank outside in expected points added per game. Their run game, on the other hand, has been abysmal. They are not just 32nd in EPA per rush, but also in attempts, yards and yards per attempt — a direct result of their offensive line being in shambles: they have used 11 different linemen this year, with seven of them playing more than 100 snaps.

Defensively, Green Bay has performed very well especially in one department: taking the ball away. No other unit in football has had a better percentage of drives ending in giveaways than the Packers', which registers takeaways on 16.7% of opponents' possessions. For comparison, the Patriots are giving the ball away at a rate of 17.9% — second-worst in the league.

The Patriots and Packers have followed the same pattern so far this year. Both lost their season openers but came back with a win the following week only to lose again in Week 3. They then rattled off three straight victories before a defeat in Week 7 and subsequent win in Week 8.

Week 1: 39-22 loss at Minnesota Vikings (0-1)Week 2: 20-17 OT win at New York Jets (1-1)Week 3: 35-14 loss vs. Atlanta Falcons (1-2)Week 4: 17-14 win at Tampa Bay Buccaneers (2-2)Week 5: 31-7 win vs. Chicago Bears (3-2)Week 6: 23-14 win vs. Dallas Cowboys (4-2)Week 7: 20-17 loss at Detroit Lions (4-3)Week 8: 27-19 win vs. Carolina Panthers (5-3)

As for the games themselves, the Packers didn't look overly impressive so far. They barely avoided going 0-3 by beating the moribund Jets in overtime, and registered one of their wins against a Bears team led by a pair of backup quarterbacks. That said, they still have the eighth-best strength of victory.

Roster up-to-date as of Nov. 4, 5 a.m. ET | *denotes nominal starter

Quarterback (2): Jordan Love* (10), Tyrod Taylor (6)

Running back (4): Josh Jacobs* (8), MarShawn Lloyd (32), Pierre Strong Jr. (22), Kaleb Johnson (26)

Wide receiver (6): Christian Watson* (9), Matthew Golden* (0), Savion Williams* (83), Bo Melton (16 | KR), J.Michael Sturdivant (87), Coleman Owen (13 | KR/PR)

Specialists (3): Trey Smack (28 | K), Daniel Whelan (19 | P/H), Matt Orzech (42 | LS)

Through the first eight weeks of the season, no quarterback has attempted more passes or thrown for more yards than Jordan Love. The seventh-year man has gone 192-for-312 (61.5%) for 2,246 yards with 16 touchdowns and six interceptions so far. He also has scored a rushing touchdown and is ranked 12th in the NFL in EPA per play (0.150).

The Packers putting the ball in Love's hand is no surprise given their aforementioned struggles running the football behind an offensive line that has been a revolving door so far. One would assume the QB himself also has been impacted by this, but his 4.3% sack rate is still fairly low and the sixth-best in football. As a consequence, Love has been able to push the ball down the field: he is tied with Drake Maye and Geno Smith as the league leader in completions of 20-plus yards (17) and tied for third in average depth of target (9.8).

Unfortunately for Love, his receiving corps has not held up its end of the bargain at times. A league-leading 23 of his passes have been dropped, resulting in the second-worst drop rate in the NFL (10.7%).

And that is despite Green Bay having some talent at the receiving positions. Christian Watson (42/708/6) and Matthew Golden (43/619/4) are among the most productive wide receiver pairings in football, while tight end Tucker Kraft (35/350/3) has also been steadily involved. Behind those three, however, there is a significant drop-off in receiving production — the passing game runs through their connection with Love.

The running game, meanwhile, doesn't run a whole lot at all. Part of it is Josh Jacobs (32/75/1) missing six games on the commissioner's exempt list due to domestic violence charges, part is neither him nor MarShawn Lloyd (57/149/2) being particularly effective behind Green Bay's O-line.

The outlook isn't much better either: starting center Sean Rhyan (ankle) and No. 2 right guard Travis Glover (knee) were absent from practice on Wednesday, while nominal right guard Jacob Monk and right tackle Zach Bako-Bewele are currently on injured reserve. Maybe some extra time coming off a mini-bye can help the unit find some chemistry, but the production on the ground so far has been poor.

Defensively, star outside linebacker Micah Parsons remains on the physically unable to perform list even after returning to practice on Wednesday. In his place, Lukas Van Ness has been the top guy on the edge: his 28 quarterback pressures are leading the team, as are his 4.5 sacks. The Packers are about more than those two, with the other edges all being heavily involved in the rotation.

On the interior, Karl Brooks, Devonte Wyatt and rookie Chris McClellan are the main three. With rotational DTs Jonathan Ford and Javon Hargrave on IR, they are hoarding snaps at the position.

Green Bay's injury questions also have hit the linebacker position: Edgerrin Cooper is out for the year, while Zaire Franklin has missed practice on Wednesday with a shin issue. If Franklin ends up missing a third straight game, Isaiah McDuffie and Ty'ron Hopper will be the main men off the ball. Hooper is one to have an eye on: his two interceptions are tied for second on the team behind only safety Xavier McKinney's three.

Speaking of McKinney, he is part of a secondary that relies heavily on three-safety sets featuring him, Evan Williams and rookie Javon Bullard. At cornerback, Keiseaon Nixon and Brandon Cisse are the starters and unlikely to leave the field in any situations. Together, the five have registered eight takeaways so far this year.

One potential area of concern for the pickers is their kicker. Rookie Trey Smack is only 11-of-16 on field goals and 16-of-19 on extra points so far this season. His combined success rate of 77.1% is the worst in the NFL among regular kickers.

Johnson (46), ED Nyjalik Kelly (47), ED Arron Mosby (53), LB Jack Dingle (48), CB Elijah Culp (39), CB Domani Jackson (20), S John Saunders Jr. (35), K Lenny Krieg (38 | exempt)

The most important name on the Packers' reserve lists entering Week 9 is four-time All-Pro selection Micah Parsons, who is recovering from an ACL tear suffered last December. While he did return to practice this week, Parsons playing on Sunday is still considered unlikely.

The star edge rusher is not the only starter sidelined. Linebacker Edgerrin Cooper will miss the remainder of the season with an Achilles injury, while wide receiver Jayden Reed is out for the remainder of the year due to a neck issue. The aforementioned Jacob Monk is on IR with a quad injury, while Zach Bako-Bewele won't come back this season from his patellar injury.

Coordinators: Adam Stenavich (OC), Jonathan Gannon (DC), Cameron Achord (ST)

Matt LaFleur has been the Packers' head coach since 2019. Not only has he gone a combined 84-49-1 over his seven-plus seasons, he also reached the playoffs six times and earned three division titles. Not only did he provide success since arriving in Green Bay, he also provided stability that extends beyond himself: offensive coordinator Adam Stenavich, for example, has been with the club since 2022.

The same cannot be said for his defensive and special teams counterparts, Jonathan Gannon and Cameron Achord — the latter a former Patriots assistant — who were both hired just this offseason. Achord is not the only New England connection in Green Bay: offensive quality control coach T.C. McCartney was the Patriots' quarterbacks coach in 2024, while outside linebackers coach, run game coordinator and defensive assistant head coach DeMarcus Covington spent eight years in Foxborough.

#2764. Bills news: What to make of Buffalo’s dominant defensive performance vs. Ravens?

The Buffalo Bills defense has been much maligned so far in the 2026 NFL season, and for good reason. Heading into a Week 8 home game vs. the Baltimore Ravens, Buffalo ranked 30th in points allowed per game (28.5) and 31st in yards per game (386.8), often struggling to stop the pass and get off the field on third down.

Then, after knocking out Lamar Jackson on the Ravens first offensive play of the game, Buffalo's defense put on a show against Baltimore's backup quarterbacks, allowing only 145 yards of total offense and just 68 passing yards while logging four sacks with 12 quarterback hits and forcing three turnovers.

Bring the energy of game day wherever you go and share every reaction with fellow members of the Bills Mafia.

Seamlessly jump between communities and conversations

Faster commenting and posting experience!

Download the SB Nation app on iOS or Android.

As great as the Bills defense fared vs. Baltimore, the level of competition does have to be considered, as Buffalo did much of its damage against second-stringer Tyler Huntley (injured after only 10 snaps), and emergency QB Joe Fagnano, an undrafted rookie making his NFL debut with little preparation.

Today's edition of Buffalo Rumblinks leads off with thoughts on whether the positives shown vs. Baltimore are sustainable for the rest of the season, or whether the results are fool's gold.

Check out the news items below and then let us know your thoughts on whether Buffalo's defense has turned a corner.

All season long, the Buffalo Bills' defense has been harping on the need to communicate better. And regardless of whether it was Lamar Jackson, Tyler Huntley, or Joe Fagnano quarterbacking the Ravens, for at least one game, Buffalo's defense excelled at communicating with each other.

Additionally, Buffalo's run defense rose to the challenge, limiting future Hall of Fame running back Derrick Henry to 60 yards from scrimmage on his 13 touches, while dynamic wide receiver Zay Flowers was held without a catch on his five targets.

Greg Rousseau and Ed Oliver were constantly in Baltimore's backfield and finished with three quarterback hits apiece, while Cole Bishop came up with a strip-sack, Rousseau, Landon Jackson and T.J. Parker each added sacks, and Davison Igbinosun came away with his first career interception after Geno Stone batted away a pass.

First-year defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard tried a few new wrinkles on Sunday, calling plays from the booth instead of on the field while guiding a defense that set season-best marks in man coverage rate (54.8%), blitz rate (61.3%), and middle-of-field closed coverages (67.7%).

"We talked about it all week, just being aggressive after coming off the bye, and we looked at things we could work on," Rousseau said. "And I feel like we did a good job of going out there and starting fast. And most importantly, finishing, because we've had good games as a defense.

Despite the positives, there are still warts on defense: the play of Buffalo's linebackers has been less than stellar; the pass rush—outside of Rousseau and Deone Walker—has been inconsistent; the secondary has battled through injuries and erratic play; and penalties continue to be an issue.

"I think our defense should look at today and understand that that's what the expectation is," Brady said. "And I'm not talking about the production. I'm not talking about the takeaways and sacks. I'm talking about the style that they played, the way that they flew around."

Only time will tell whether the Bills defense is finally starting to gel under Leonhard, or whether Buffalo just took advantage of a banged-up Ravens offense.

#2763. Chasing the Final 4: Wildcats, Bulldogs in quarterfinals

Kelly Houle knew what last name to look out for before turning on Hardin's film.

In the late '90s, Houle coached against the Bulldogs' quarterback Cale Nedens' dad Chris in wrestling. Now he's watching Cale slip out of the hands of tacklers and wondering how many Wildcats it'll take to contain him.

Nedens is the reigning Class A wrestling champion at 150 pounds; he brings the Bulldogs (8-2) to Columbia Falls (7-1) for a quarterfinal matchup at 7 p.m. on Friday. The Wildcats earned a first-round bye with their second straight Northwest A title. Hardin beat Lewistown 22-14 on the road for its first playoff win in 14 years.

Houle and his staff charted 61 runs in 70 plays in Hardin's victory over Lewistown. By Houle's count, Nedens carried the ball 42 times for about 300 yards.

"They just found something they liked," Houle said. "They kept doing it and doing it, and they were successful."

Houle likened Hardin's attack to a Wildcat offense. Nedens takes the snap and looks for a crease, and a play that seems bottled up can turn into a long run. He can throw it, too. In a 30-22 win over Dawson County, Nedens passed for 111 yards to go with 245 rushing yards and three scores on the ground.

"He has a tendency to get in there, bounce around, all of a sudden he squeaks out the other side," said Houle.

Staying in their gaps will be a priority for linebacker Trip Ross and the Wildcats. When Columbia Falls has the ball, Ross gives Hardin a runner to worry about, too.

Ross ran 11 times for 114 yards, including a 51-yard touchdown, in a 42-0 win over Libby to close the regular season. He also caught one of Banyan Johnston's four touchdown passes. Johnston threw for 212 yards and ran for a score, and Jory Hill caught five passes for 118 yards and two touchdowns.

Houle sees room for Hill and the other slot receivers between Hardin's linebackers and safeties. He also wants to use Johnston's legs more in the playoffs, giving the Wildcats another option alongside Ross.

"We're just going to take advantage of the green grass that they give us," he said..

Columbia Falls spent most of its bye week cleaning up its own play. Houle liked what he saw enough to give the Wildcats an unofficial record through five sessions.

Friday's winner will face the winner of Frenchtown at Sidney in the semifinals. Frenchtown handed Columbia Falls its only loss, 28-13 on Sept. 4.

Brett Bollweg watched the East Helena Vigilantes' quarterback run and their receivers stretch the field. He recognized a few things from his own sideline.

"It feels a little bit like us," said Bollweg.

The Bulldogs (9-1) visit East Helena (7-1) at 7 p.m. on Friday. Both teams took their only loss by three points this season against Columbia Falls.

The winner of Friday's matchup will face either Billings Central or Hamilton in the Class A semifinals.

The Vigilantes ran for 419 yards in their 34-14 win over Lewistown to clinch the Central A title. Running back Leo Longcake carried the ball 36 times for 215 yards, and quarterback Bearek Shuman ran for three touchdowns, including a 60-yard score. Bollweg also singled out receivers Conor Carpenter and Parker Taylor for what they can do downfield.

"They run the ball well," Bollweg said. "They're good up front."

Whitefish leaned on its own front in last week's 36-12 win over Dillon, running for 248 yards and finishing with 449 yards of offense. Luke Dalen completed 17 of 23 passes for 201 yards and a touchdown and ran 15 times for 108 yards and three scores. Vance Schwaiger added 104 yards on 19 carries, including a 23-yard touchdown. Keenan Curtiss caught three passes for 56 yards, including the screen that put Whitefish ahead for good.

"Up front is where we won the game tonight," said Bollweg after the Dillon win.

This week, Bollweg sees an East Helena defense whose linebackers play downhill. He said Whitefish can use some of that aggression to its advantage with plays already in the book.

Dillon led 12-7 early in the second quarter before Whitefish scored the final 29 points.

If Friday's game is close late, Bollweg likes how his team has handled those moments this season. He pointed to tight games against Hamilton and Columbia Falls and the way the Bulldogs responded when they fell behind Dillon last week.

"There was never a moment where our guys panicked," Bollweg said. "There was never a moment where our guys flinched."

Campbell released a statement on Wednesday, indicating that he is progressing well in his recovery from the injury (via Pride of Detroit):

My family and I want to sincerely thank everyone for the overwhelming amount of love, prayers, and support we've received over the past few days. It means more to us than words can express.

I'm incredibly encouraged by the progress I've made in such a short period of time. I have full movement in my lower body, and I'm continuing to make progress with movement in my upper body. I know there's still work ahead, but I remain very optimistic. I'm taking things one day at a time, staying positive, and focusing on getting better.

My faith in God has never been stronger. I know He has a plan for me, and I trust in that plan. I know there may be challenges ahead, but with my faith, my family, and so many people in my corner, I know we'll get through this.

I especially want to thank the athletic trainers and medical personnel who responded and cared for me on the field. I know those were difficult moments, and I'm incredibly grateful for the professionalism, compassion, and care you showed me. The way you handled everything and looked after me when I needed it most is something I'll never forget. From the bottom of my heart, thank you.

I also can't say enough about the incredible care I've received from the medical team at Henry Ford Hospital and the Detroit Lions medical staff. They've been amazing to me and my family throughout this process, and I'm truly grateful for everything they've done.

To my teammates, coaches, and everyone in the Lions organization, I want you to know how much I love and appreciate you. This team is a family to me, and the way everyone has been there for me means everything. I'm proud to be a Detroit Lion and couldn't ask to be surrounded by a better group of people.

One thing I've learned about Detroit is that this city is built on toughness, resilience, and grit. That's exactly how I'm going to approach this challenge.

Please continue to keep me and my family in your prayers. We feel the love, and I can't thank everyone enough.

Campbell is on the injury report as a non-participant, as the Lions have not moved him to injured reserve yet, but none of that matters. It is just great news to hear that he has full lower-body movement and is progressing with his upper body.

#2758. Bills Mafia’s Week 9 rooting interests come with a few sacrifices

That was an interesting weekend of football. The Buffalo Bills won, although I'm still trying to figure out how. Seems like that's happened a lot this season, but, hey, no one ever claimed being a member of Bills Mafia was easy.

Anyway, the Bills won. The Chiefs lost. And, as tough as being a Bills fan can be, there may have been a little sweetness in seeing Patrick Mahomes holding the ball when the clock hit zero, unable to get the job done.

Really, the only thing that could have made Week 8 any better would have been a Patriots loss. But they say beggars can't be choosers, and when it comes to New England, the only team to have bested the Bills up to this point, we have to be beggars. At least until Week 13, when Allen and Co. get a chance to even the score.

When the dust settled and the lights went out in stadiums across the league Sunday night, the Buffalo Bills were sitting alone atop the AFC. And that sure looked nice.

So, let's take a look at who we, as members of Bills Mafia, need to be rooting for this weekend. After all, there's a lot of football to be played before the Bills take the field Monday night, and we need something to do while we wait.

_____________________________________________________________________________

_____________________________________________________________________________

Buffalo Bills at Minnesota Vikings Root for: Bills

The Bills have worked their way to the top of the AFC, and now the job is to stay there. A win in Minnesota would keep Buffalo in control of its own path toward the No. 1 seed, regardless of what happens around the league on Sunday. Go Bills!

Green Bay Packers at New England Patriots Root for: Packers

The Patriots are the only team to have beaten Buffalo this season, and they're still the biggest threat to the Bills in the AFC East. New England also holds the head-to-head tiebreaker, at least until the two meet again in Week 13. A Packers win would give Buffalo a little more breathing room at the top of the division. Go Pack Go!

Detroit Lions at Miami Dolphins Root for: Lions

Miami is sitting at the bottom of the AFC East with just one win, and there's no reason to help the Dolphins climb out of that hole. A Detroit win keeps another division rival further behind Buffalo, and that's good enough for us.

New York Jets at Kansas City Chiefs Root for: Jets

Yes, we're rooting for the Jets. Kansas City is still a threat to Buffalo's hold on the top spot in the AFC, and another Chiefs loss would go a long way toward keeping the Bills there. The Jets, meanwhile, are far enough behind Buffalo that we can afford to let them have this one. Just this once. J-E-T-S! JETS! JETS! JETS!

_____________________________________________________________________________

Jacksonville Jaguars at Baltimore Ravens Root for: Ravens

Jacksonville is a little too close to Buffalo in the AFC standings for comfort, so we'd like to see the Jaguars pick up another loss. And since the Bills just beat Baltimore, a Ravens win gives Buffalo a little boost in strength of victory. Two birds, one stone. And we don't even have to like the Ravens — or whoever they have under center.

Cincinnati Bengals at Atlanta Falcons Root for: Falcons

The Bengals are sitting at 5-2, and that's a little closer to the top of the AFC than we'd like. Atlanta can do us a favor here by handing Cincinnati its third loss. Nothing complicated about this one.

Denver Broncos at Carolina Panthers Root for: Panthers

Denver is sitting right behind Buffalo in the AFC standings, and we'd really like to put another game between the two. Yes, a Broncos loss hurts the Bills' strength of schedule, but with Buffalo and Denver set for a Christmas Day showdown, we'd be happy to see the Panthers play the part of the Grinch in November.

Dallas Cowboys at Indianapolis Colts Root for: Colts

The Colts aren't going anywhere in the AFC standings right now, but that doesn't mean they can't do us a favor. Indianapolis traded its 2027 first-round pick to the Jets, and the more games the Colts win, the worse that pick gets. The last thing we need is New York getting its hands on a franchise-changing player with the first pick in the draft.

Cleveland Browns at New Orleans Saints Root for: Saints

The Browns are sitting at 5-3, and that's close enough to the top of the AFC for us to want them to stay right where they are. Or, better yet, take another step backward. New Orleans hasn't exactly been setting the world on fire, but we're not asking the Saints to win the Super Bowl. Just one game on Sunday will do.

Houston Texans at Los Angeles Chargers Root for: Chargers

The Chargers are 0-7, and the last thing we need is for them to turn that miserable season into the first overall pick in next year's draft. So, we're rooting for Los Angeles to finally get a win. Come on, Chargers. Surely you can manage just one.

Las Vegas Raiders at San Francisco 49ers Root for: Raiders

Buffalo already has a win over Las Vegas in the books, so another Raiders win would give the Bills a little help with strength of victory. Strange how quickly a team can go from an opponent to a temporary friend.

_____________________________________________________________________________

Los Angeles Rams over Washington Commanders — Strength of Victory

Chicago Bears over Tampa Bay Buccaneers — Strength of schedule.

_____________________________________________________________________________

_____________________________________________________________________________

Being at the top of the AFC is a pretty good place to be. The problem is, now we're going to spend the rest of the season looking over our shoulders to see who's coming for that No. 1 seed.

This weekend, we'll be keeping one eye on the Patriots, another on the Chiefs, and somehow finding a way to root for the Jets without feeling too dirty about it. Being a Bills fan sometimes requires sacrifices.

And if Sunday goes our way, a Buffalo win on Monday night would just be the icing on the cake.

#2757. The WNBA spent 30 years just trying to prove it belonged. Now it’s time to build daringly

The wildest of the WNBA's 30 seasons ended in defiant triumph. It ended with evidence that the league is greater than the labor battles, culture wars and institutional missteps. It ended with a gnarly defensive finals lasting seven games and holding interest all the way to a record-setting television audience for Game 7.

It ended with the Golden State Valkyries, a newbie full of substance, capturing the title in their second year. And it ended with coach Natalie Nakase, a 5-foot-2 former UCLA walk-on, standing atop women's basketball and delivering a message about her team that resonated with the entire sport.

"This is for all the people that have been underrated, misunderstood," she said. "This is for all y'all, because this is proof: If you put your heart and all your soul, you can (expletive) win championships!"

After a taxing season, there couldn't have been a more perfect final scene: confetti and F-bombs bursting in air.

Two nights before that cinematic ending, the Valkyries-Atlanta Dream series played Game 6 at 12:30 p.m. on a Thursday because of drama and suspect planning over arena availability. Nobody wanted a lunch-hour conclusion in Atlanta, and fortunately, it wasn't the final impression this season. Despite the confusion and criticism, that penultimate moment still managed to be compelling.

Now, let's put both images side by side: Game 7 averaged 3.3 million viewers, the most-watched WNBA playoff game, and Game 6 averaged 1.5 million, a robust number even though office workers needed to sneak glances on their phones. That exemplified the WNBA in 2026. Two extremes stirred endless debate. Yet the sport won anyway.

That shouldn't be viewed as a crisis. It's a growth spurt. The league is wearing clothes that no longer fit. Now that another consequential offseason has arrived, with a vacant commissioner job and a handful of leadership jobs open at high-profile franchises, there's time to revamp the wardrobe.

For the past few years, as leaguewide popularity has risen, critics have pointed to various controversies as proof of an unserious league: the ugly moments of a labor fight that dragged into March before resulting in a landmark new collective bargaining agreement; the players' denunciation of the leadership style of retiring commissioner Cathy Engelbert; the ongoing perception of jealousy over Caitlin Clark's popularity; the feud between newcomers who worship Clark and longtime loyalists with a broader view of the league; a manufactured culture war over transgender players (even though the league has none) that turned courtside seats into stages for provocateurs.

Those critics have some evidence, for sure, but their conclusion is off the mark. Unserious leagues don't matter this much to people. Much of the drama wasn't a sign of a clown show. It was an indicator of growth the league wanted but never fully prepared to handle.

For a long time, the league survived by doubting itself, by hedging its bets. From now on, it will thrive by believing.

Not surface-level confidence. Complete self-assurance. Ambition to maximize progress.

Look at what's no longer in question. The salary cap went from $1.5 million to $7 million. Ratings and attendance numbers are surging. The Golden State franchise is worth $1 billion two seasons into its launch. Clark hasn't arrived as a savior. She has been an amplifier. The survival question that has hung over the WNBA since 1997 doesn't need to be asked anymore.

The greatest fix the WNBA can make isn't really a fix. It's a shift in mentality. The league doesn't need repair anymore. Maybe it never did.

For three decades, the product has been better than its reputation. The basketball was good when crowds were sparse and TV execs were offering scraps. Skeptics, many of whom never watched and lazily repeated the assumption that women's sports could only survive as charity, mistook neglect for a judgment. The WNBA absorbed that doubt and built a safe space for protection. It had to be careful, cost-conscious and grateful for the tiniest bit of acknowledgment. That approach kept the league alive. Now, those remnants hold it back.

It's noticeable in the hedging. The WNBA took too many trepidatious stances on major issues, whether it was trans eligibility, policing nasty fan behavior or ensuring finals-worthy buildings were available. When the WNBA had less to lose, it took bolder positions, especially during the pandemic-era days of heavy collaboration with the players. Lately, it has been afraid to establish a clear identity, mostly because a diverse audience is contributing to this boom. But every time the league tiptoed, someone else filled the gap and co-opted the story. And those people never have the sport's best interest at heart.

Golden State represents the sleekest new model of what it means to meet this moment. The Valkyries haven't hedged. They went big from the start: turning the Chase Center into Ballhalla, sellouts and season ticket holders galore, a culture deliberately built around a coach and a roster that plays like a team rather than a collection of parts around a marquee superstar. They functioned like a major-league franchise before anyone permitted them. Now, they're champions. Already, they're champions. But that trophy didn't make them successful. It was the culmination of their breakthrough. They're the trendy avatar for what belief looks like.

The Valkyries aren't alone. Franchises such as the Las Vegas Aces, New York Liberty and Seattle Storm have spent years outpacing the league in ambition, investing in facilities, staff and continuity and becoming model franchises. Under new ownership, the Phoenix Mercury are getting to that level, too. No operation is more stable than the Minnesota Lynx. The Indiana Fever, who endured a long stretch as one of the league's worst-run organizations, are finally rising structurally to Clark's level of transcendence. With a team president and general manager to hire, they could complete their transformation. The Dream, a franchise once known more for turmoil than basketball, ended this season with the best kind of problem: too much demand for its building to hold. The Dallas Wings look like they could be next. Or maybe the Washington Mystics, another good organization that won the title in 2019 and is currently stocked with enviable talent, are a budding dynasty.

A couple of franchises are struggling, but the general message throughout the league appears to be the same. Ambition isn't as risky as it used to be. The teams that bet big on the WNBA are winning the bet. The league office should go all in, too.

That's the task for Engelbert's successor. The league doesn't need a caretaker or a crisis manager. It doesn't need a CEO above all other skills. It needs someone who believes fully and builds daringly. No need to be reckless, but this is now a maximizer's job. Assume sellouts rather than hope for them. Draft and articulate a league-wide code of conduct so that the protection of players and fans isn't dependent on which arena hosts the game. Box out the provocateurs by taking proactive measures to eliminate blind spots.

And this one is for Adam Silver and the NBA owners he serves: Empower a commissioner with greater autonomy to make decisions in the WNBA's interests, even when they don't align perfectly with the NBA's.

None of this is radical. It just requires the league to stop acting as if one wrong investment will make it disappear.

Believing at this level carries risk. But the WNBA has spent 30 seasons managing risk. The bigger danger now is not being ambitious enough.

Engelbert deserves credit for navigating all of this and putting the league in a strong position, including an aggressive plan to expand to 18 teams by 2030 that has yielded incredible early returns. Her successor must be asked to do more than maintain. The opportunity exists to lift the WNBA out of the niche tier permanently.

The WNBA has spent three decades proving it was underrated. That part is over.

It's time to shop for a new look, one fitting a league that knew it was always destined to be fashionable.

#2756. Packers-Patriots Preview: Christian Gonzalez defines New England’s defense

Last week, the Carolina Panthers sat in split-safety coverages against the Green Bay Packers, forcing the team to run the football or take checkdown passes routinely — just like their matchup in 2025. While this didn't stop the Packers' offense, which still had a 100-yard receiver in Christian Watson despite his in-game trip to the hospital for a rib injury, it did mean that the offense was a lot less explosive than it was in prior weeks.

Don't expect that same strategy from the New England Patriots this week, as it's not really their identity to sit back and just let offense happen to them, hoping that the opposing team will trip up at some point.

According to Next Gen Stats, the Patriots have sent max pressure (six or more pass rushers) with man coverage behind it 37 times already this season, the most in the league. On those looks, they've posted five sacks and allowed just 14 completions on 31 pass attempts (45 percent) for 123 yards (4.0 yards per attempt), with one interception and no touchdowns surrendered. The overall conversion rate on those players is 21.6 percent, which is the best mark in the league in these situations.

In contrast, New England has only sent 13 of these "max pressure" looks out of zone in 2026, surrendering 9 of 13 in the air for 131 yards (10 yards per attempt) and a touchdown. In short, the Patriots' man coverage looks have been better for them than zone coverage looks this year, especially when they're trying to speed quarterbacks up.

Patriots cornerback Christian Gonzalez, their All-Pro defender, helps the team unlock that man coverage identity when so many other NFL teams are leaning out of the man coverage game. When Gonzalez has been on the field, the team has played man coverage on 39 percent of their defensive snaps, compared to just 29 percent when he's not in the game.

Packers quarterback Jordan Love has done his most damage this year against the blitz when he's had either Christian Watson or Matthew Golden in one-on-one looks, but unlike a lot of the teams Green Bay has played this year, the Patriots are just as comfortable playing man as they are playing zone, even behind a blitz.

Gonzalez travels, as he's followed around specific receivers in man coverage at least 10 times in three separate games, a number that leads the NFL. For perspective, neither Watson nor Golden has been seen man coverage 10 times by a single defender in a single game this entire season.

Something has to break here. This is going to be the most important matchup of Sunday's game, by far. The only question is whether Gonzalez will travel with a receiver and which one of the Packers' deep threats it will be.

#2755. Watch Victor Wembanyama's historic night: 52 points, 24 rebounds, eight blocks

It was a legendary performance, even by Victor Wembanyama's unreasonably lofty standards: A career-high 52 points and 24 rebounds, plus eight blocked shots.

It's been 52 years since a player put up a stat line like that — and Wembanyama did that despite fighting off a virus and tweaking his ankle in the fourth quarter.The Spurs needed every bit of an epic Wemby game to beat Dallas, 112-111.

Wembanyama went 16-of-28 from the floor and did much of his damage at the free-throw line, where he was 19-of-23. The only knock on his night was that he shot 1-of-8 from 3, but he realized that and got downhill. Wemby finished 14-of-18 in the paint.

"I can still do more," Wembanyama said postgame, via the Associated Press. "I mean, my shots weren't falling tonight and that forces me into a style of play that is exhausting. I can do it. I mean the proof is here. I can do it, but I can be much better if my shots fall. I know it's just a matter of time."

Wemby's hot night started early, he had 29 points, 15 rebounds and five blocks in the first half — the first player since the NBA's play-by-play era started in 1996 with at least 25 points, 10 rebounds and five blocks in a half.

After dropping their first two games of the season, the Spurs have rattled off five straight wins and Wembanyama has inserted himself in the too-early MVP conversation next to Luka Doncic.

#2754. Stanford's Jay Leng Jr. breaks new ground with WWT sponsorship

Jay Leng Jr. has gone through plenty of changes in the past three months.

The junior at Stanford won the Western Amateur and then finished runner-up at the U.S. Amateur. He later represented the red, white and blue on the U.S. Walker Cup team in Ireland. Oh, and he made his PGA Tour debut.

Now, he's breaking barriers in the Name, Image and Likeness space.

World Wide Technology, which is sponsoring this week's PGA Tour event at El Cardonal in Cabo San Lucas, Mexico, has partnered with Leng on an NIL deal that will see him wear the WWT logo on his apparel at all PGA Tour and non-collegiate sanctioned events. Leng is the eighth golfer to don the WWT logo but first amateur to do so.

"I'm really excited to be their first NIL ambassador," Leng said. "I know it's not easy to trust a 21-year-old to be an ambassador, but I am glad they see a future for me and I'm grateful for the opportunities."

Other WWT golf ambassadors include Billy Andrade, Ben Griffin, Luke Donald, Austin Eckroat, Keith Mitchell, Taylor Pendrith and Justin Suh. Griffin is the defending champion at the WWT Championship.

Matt Horner, the Executive Vice President of WWT, told Golfweek the way Leng carried himself and the opportunities he presented with a partnership were too good to pass up.

Leng will wear the logo at the Masters Tournament and the U.S. Open at Pebble Beach next year. That, in addition to whatever amateur accolades he may collect in the time being, was a perfect opportunity for partnership.

More: These 6 amateurs earned invites to the 2027 Masters

"I think it's great for us to be able to partner with an athlete like this early on," Horner said. "We're excited to see Jay blossom and continue to grow."

Leng is making his second PGA Tour start this week at El Cardonal looking for his first made cut. He'll do so with a new sponsor on his clothing.
